Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(a) Observers.** An **observer at $p$** is a tangent vector
$n\in T_pM$ such that $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ is future-directed in the sense of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], that is, $g_p(n,N_p)<0$. Because
$g_p(n,n)=-1\neq0$, an observer is timelike and in particular nonzero
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). Observers at $p$ exist:
the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and
$n:=N_p/\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}$ satisfies $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and
$g_p(n,N_p)=-\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}<0$, where the square root is the
nonnegative root of [[def-rational-power]]; then $-n$ is a unit timelike
vector with $g_p(-n,N_p)>0$, so it is not an observer, and the two vectors
$n,-n$ point in opposite time directions.

**(b) Rest space.** For an observer $n$ at $p$, the **rest space** of $n$ is
the $g_p$-orthogonal complement of the line $\mathbb Rn$,

$$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM: g_p(v,n)=0\},$$

in the sense of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. It is
a linear subspace of $T_pM$. The further facts that $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and
that the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive definite are proved
in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]; they are consequences, not
part of the definition.

**(c) Spatial projection.** The **spatial projection** of the observer $n$ is
the map

$$h_n:T_pM\longrightarrow T_pM,\qquad h_n(v):=v+g_p(n,v)\,n .$$

The map is linear because $g_p$ is bilinear, its image is contained in
$n^{\perp}$, and it fixes $n^{\perp}$ pointwise; that it is the
$g_p$-orthogonal projection onto $n^{\perp}$ with kernel $\mathbb Rn$ is
proved in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]].

**(d) Scope.** An observer at $p$ is a single tangent vector. It is not an
ordered basis or frame of $T_pM$, not a chart, not a field of observers such as
the congruences defined later on this page, and not a curve or a worldline: no
parametrized curve, clock reading, proper time or measurement is attached to
$n$ by this definition. The physical reading of an observer as the direction
of an ideal clock's worldline, and the measurement interpretation of the
observer-relative quantities introduced later on this page, belong to the
physical postulates and unit conventions of the framework and are not asserted
here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). The cotangent space $T_p^*M$ is
the algebraic dual of $T_pM$ ([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]).

**Musical isomorphisms.** Define the **flat map**

$$\flat_p:T_pM\longrightarrow T_p^*M,\qquad \flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot),$$

so that $\flat_p(v)(w)=g_p(v,w)$; it is $\mathbb R$-linear by bilinearity of
$g_p$. Its kernel is $\{v:g_p(v,w)=0\text{ for all }w\}=\{0\}$ because $g_p$ is
nondegenerate, and $\dim_{\mathbb R}T_pM=\dim_{\mathbb R}T_p^*M=4$ since the
coordinate derivations of a chart form a basis of $T_pM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]); hence
$\flat_p$ is a linear isomorphism and has an inverse
$\sharp_p:T_p^*M\to T_pM$.

**Inverse metric.** The **inverse metric** at $p$ is the symmetric bilinear form

$$g_p^{-1}:T_p^*M\times T_p^*M\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta).$$

It is symmetric because $g_p$ is, and it is nondegenerate: if
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta)=0$ for all $\beta$, then $g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\cdot)=0$,
so $\sharp_p\alpha=0$ and hence $\alpha=0$.

**Components in a chart.** Let $(U,x)$ be a smooth chart and
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ the components of $g$; let
$dx^a|_q$ be the differential of the coordinate function $x^a$ at $q$
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]), so that
$dx^a|_q(\partial_b|_q)=\partial_b|_q(x^a)=\delta^a{}_b$. Define the components
of the inverse metric in this chart by

$$g^{ab}(q):=g_q^{-1}\bigl(dx^a|_q,\,dx^b|_q\bigr),\qquad q\in U,$$

so that $\sharp_q(dx^a|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)\,\partial_b|_q$; equivalently
$(g^{ab}(q))$ is the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab}(q))$ at every $q$, that is

$$g^{ac}(q)\,g_{cb}(q)=\delta^a{}_b,\qquad g_{ac}(q)g^{cb}(q)=\delta_a{}^b,$$

because $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=dx^a|_q(\partial_c|_q)=\delta^a{}_c$
and also $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)g_{bc}(q)$. In
particular $g^{ab}=g^{ba}$. The components $g^{ab}$ depend smoothly on $q$;
this is proved in [[lem-gr-inverse-metric-is-smooth]].

**Raising, lowering and metric trace.** Let $A$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on an open set $V\subseteq M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). At each $p\in V$ define the
endomorphism

$$A^\sharp_p:T_pM\to T_pM,\qquad A^\sharp_p(v):=\sharp_p\bigl(A_p(v,\cdot)\bigr),$$

characterized by $g_p(A^\sharp_p(v),w)=A_p(v,w)$ for all $w\in T_pM$; it is
self-adjoint for $g_p$ because $A_p$ is symmetric. Its **metric trace** is

$$\operatorname{tr}_g(A)(p):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(A^\sharp_p\bigr)$$

with the trace of an endomorphism as in [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. In a
chart the raised, mixed and doubly raised components are

$$A^{ab}:=g^{ac}g^{bd}A_{cd},\qquad A^a{}_b:=g^{ac}A_{cb},\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{tr}_g(A)=g^{ab}A_{ab},$$

the last identity obtained by evaluating in a $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, where $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ by
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] so that
$g^{ab}A_{ab}=\sum_a g^{aa}A_{aa}=-A(e_0,e_0)+A(e_1,e_1)+A(e_2,e_2)+A(e_3,e_3)$,
which is the trace of the endomorphism $v\mapsto\sharp_p(A_p(v,\cdot))$ in that
basis. All these operations are pointwise and depend only on $g$, $A$ and the
duality pairing, not on a chart.

**Conventions.** Raising and lowering apply to one index at a time and preserve
index order; $A_{ab}$, $A^a{}_b$ and $A^{ab}$ denote the same tensor $A$ with
indices positioned by $g$. The musical isomorphisms and the inverse metric are
defined for every smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of this library; no choice
principle is used in this definition, every ingredient being pointwise linear
algebra over $\mathbb R$ together with the pointwise nondegeneracy of $g_p$.

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]), with smooth atlas
$\mathcal A$ and maximal smooth atlas $[\mathcal A]$
([[def-smooth-atlas]], [[def-smoothly-compatible-charts]]). For $p\in M$ the
tangent space $T_pM$ is the real vector space of derivations at $p$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]), and the cotangent space is its
algebraic dual $T_p^*M:=(T_pM)^*$
([[def-cotangent-space-and-cotangent-bundle-as-a-disjoint-union]]).

A **covariant $2$-tensor at $p$** is a bilinear map
$A_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$. It is **symmetric** when
$A_p(v,w)=A_p(w,v)$ for all $v,w\in T_pM$, and **nondegenerate** when the only
$v\in T_pM$ with $A_p(v,w)=0$ for all $w\in T_pM$ is $v=0$.

A **smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$** is a family $A=(A_p)_{p\in M}$
assigning to each $p$ a covariant $2$-tensor $A_p$ at $p$, such that for every
chart $(U,x)$ of the maximal smooth atlas $[\mathcal A]$ the **component
functions**

$$A_{ab}(q):=A_q\!\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^a}\Big|_q,\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x^b}\Big|_q\right),\qquad q\in U,$$

are $C^\infty$ on $U$. Here $\partial/\partial x^a|_q$ is the coordinate
derivation at $q$ ([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]],
[[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), the index
ranges over the label set $I_n=\{1,\dots,n\}$ (or the relabelled set
$I_4=\{0,1,2,3\}$ when $n=4$), and smoothness of the real-valued functions
$A_{ab}$ on the open set $U\subseteq M$ is the notion of
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]] applied to $M$ and
$\mathbb R$.

For a coordinate tuple $z\in x(U)$ define the **coordinate representative**
$A^x_{ab}(z):=A_{ab}(x^{-1}(z))$. When the argument is a coordinate tuple,
$A_{ab}(z)$ abbreviates this representative in the named chart; when it is a
point of $M$, it denotes the component function on the chart domain. Thus
$A_{ab}(x(y^{-1}(u)))$ in a change-of-coordinates formula means
$A^x_{ab}((x\circ y^{-1})(u))$, never evaluation of a function on $M$ at a
tuple. For $n=4$, $x^a$ and $\partial_a$ mean the original coordinate and
derivation labelled $a+1$, respectively; this relabels every slot and sum.
The label $0$ alone gives no coordinate vector a causal character.

Because the coordinate derivations at $q$ form a basis of $T_qM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), specifying
$A$ is the same as specifying the matrix of component functions in each chart;
[[lem-gr-covariant-two-tensor-transformation-law]] proves that the smoothness
requirement is independent of the chart used, so that the condition may be
checked on any smooth atlas of $M$, and derives the transformation law relating
components in two overlapping charts.

The field is **symmetric** when $A_p$ is symmetric for every $p\in M$, which in
a chart is the identity $A_{ab}=A_{ba}$ of component functions; it is
**nondegenerate** when $A_p$ is nondegenerate for every $p$, which in a chart is
the nonvanishing at every point of the polynomial function
$\det(A_{ab})$ of the components. The **matrix** of $A$ in a chart means the
matrix $\bigl(A_{ab}(q)\bigr)$ of its component functions at $q$.

**Convention.** In the four-dimensional case $n=4$ used in this library, indices
are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ with $0$ the time-coordinate label when such a coordinate is chosen, and we write
$A_{ab}$ for the components. A covariant $2$-tensor field is also called a
**$(0,2)$ tensor field**.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Two vectors $u,v\in V$ are
**$\eta$-orthogonal**, written $u\perp v$, when $\eta(u,v)=0$. For a subset
$S\subseteq V$ the **orthogonal complement** of $S$ is

$$S^{\perp}:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,s)=0\text{ for every }s\in S\},$$

and for a vector $u$ one writes $u^{\perp}:=\{u\}^{\perp}$.

**Elementary properties.** For every subset $S\subseteq V$:

- $S^{\perp}$ is a linear subspace of $V$: if $v,w\in S^{\perp}$ and
  $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, then for every $s\in S$ bilinearity gives
  $\eta(v+\lambda w,s)=\eta(v,s)+\lambda\eta(w,s)=0$, so $v+\lambda w\in S^{\perp}$.
  In particular the zero vector lies in $S^{\perp}$ and $S^{\perp}$ is never
  empty.
- $S\subseteq (S^{\perp})^{\perp}$: if $s\in S$, then $\eta(v,s)=0$ for every
  $v\in S^{\perp}$ by the definition of $S^{\perp}$, and symmetry of $\eta$
  gives $\eta(s,v)=0$ for every $v\in S^{\perp}$, that is,
  $s\in(S^{\perp})^{\perp}$.
- $S^{\perp}=(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}$: the inclusion
  $S\subseteq\operatorname{span}S$ gives
  $(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}\subseteq S^{\perp}$; conversely, if
  $v\in S^{\perp}$ and $u=\sum_i\lambda_i s_i$ is a finite linear combination
  with $s_i\in S$, then linearity in the second argument gives
  $\eta(v,u)=\sum_i\lambda_i\eta(v,s_i)=0$, so $v\in(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}$.

In particular, for every $u\in V$ one has $u\in u^{\perp}$ exactly when
$\eta(u,u)=0$, that is, exactly when $u$ is null or $u=0$
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

**A nonzero vector can be orthogonal to itself.** Take a basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal with
diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$; such a basis exists by clause 2 of the definition
of a Lorentz form. Then $v:=e_0+e_1$ is nonzero while
$\eta(v,v)=\eta(e_0,e_0)+2\eta(e_0,e_1)+\eta(e_1,e_1)=-1+0+1=0$, so
$v\in v^{\perp}$ with $v\neq 0$. This is exactly what fails for a
positive-definite inner product and is why orthogonal complements in a Lorentz
vector space need not be positive definite.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). The cotangent space $T_p^*M$ is
the algebraic dual of $T_pM$ ([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]).

**Musical isomorphisms.** Define the **flat map**

$$\flat_p:T_pM\longrightarrow T_p^*M,\qquad \flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot),$$

so that $\flat_p(v)(w)=g_p(v,w)$; it is $\mathbb R$-linear by bilinearity of
$g_p$. Its kernel is $\{v:g_p(v,w)=0\text{ for all }w\}=\{0\}$ because $g_p$ is
nondegenerate, and $\dim_{\mathbb R}T_pM=\dim_{\mathbb R}T_p^*M=4$ since the
coordinate derivations of a chart form a basis of $T_pM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]); hence
$\flat_p$ is a linear isomorphism and has an inverse
$\sharp_p:T_p^*M\to T_pM$.

**Inverse metric.** The **inverse metric** at $p$ is the symmetric bilinear form

$$g_p^{-1}:T_p^*M\times T_p^*M\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta).$$

It is symmetric because $g_p$ is, and it is nondegenerate: if
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta)=0$ for all $\beta$, then $g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\cdot)=0$,
so $\sharp_p\alpha=0$ and hence $\alpha=0$.

**Components in a chart.** Let $(U,x)$ be a smooth chart and
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ the components of $g$; let
$dx^a|_q$ be the differential of the coordinate function $x^a$ at $q$
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]), so that
$dx^a|_q(\partial_b|_q)=\partial_b|_q(x^a)=\delta^a{}_b$. Define the components
of the inverse metric in this chart by

$$g^{ab}(q):=g_q^{-1}\bigl(dx^a|_q,\,dx^b|_q\bigr),\qquad q\in U,$$

so that $\sharp_q(dx^a|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)\,\partial_b|_q$; equivalently
$(g^{ab}(q))$ is the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab}(q))$ at every $q$, that is

$$g^{ac}(q)\,g_{cb}(q)=\delta^a{}_b,\qquad g_{ac}(q)g^{cb}(q)=\delta_a{}^b,$$

because $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=dx^a|_q(\partial_c|_q)=\delta^a{}_c$
and also $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)g_{bc}(q)$. In
particular $g^{ab}=g^{ba}$. The components $g^{ab}$ depend smoothly on $q$;
this is proved in [[lem-gr-inverse-metric-is-smooth]].

**Raising, lowering and metric trace.** Let $A$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on an open set $V\subseteq M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). At each $p\in V$ define the
endomorphism

$$A^\sharp_p:T_pM\to T_pM,\qquad A^\sharp_p(v):=\sharp_p\bigl(A_p(v,\cdot)\bigr),$$

characterized by $g_p(A^\sharp_p(v),w)=A_p(v,w)$ for all $w\in T_pM$; it is
self-adjoint for $g_p$ because $A_p$ is symmetric. Its **metric trace** is

$$\operatorname{tr}_g(A)(p):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(A^\sharp_p\bigr)$$

with the trace of an endomorphism as in [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. In a
chart the raised, mixed and doubly raised components are

$$A^{ab}:=g^{ac}g^{bd}A_{cd},\qquad A^a{}_b:=g^{ac}A_{cb},\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{tr}_g(A)=g^{ab}A_{ab},$$

the last identity obtained by evaluating in a $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, where $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ by
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] so that
$g^{ab}A_{ab}=\sum_a g^{aa}A_{aa}=-A(e_0,e_0)+A(e_1,e_1)+A(e_2,e_2)+A(e_3,e_3)$,
which is the trace of the endomorphism $v\mapsto\sharp_p(A_p(v,\cdot))$ in that
basis. All these operations are pointwise and depend only on $g$, $A$ and the
duality pairing, not on a chart.

**Conventions.** Raising and lowering apply to one index at a time and preserve
index order; $A_{ab}$, $A^a{}_b$ and $A^{ab}$ denote the same tensor $A$ with
indices positioned by $g$. The musical isomorphisms and the inverse metric are
defined for every smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of this library; no choice
principle is used in this definition, every ingredient being pointwise linear
algebra over $\mathbb R$ together with the pointwise nondegeneracy of $g_p$.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold $M$ admits a smooth nonnegative function $h:M\to[0,\infty)$ whose closed sublevel sets are compact. In particular $h$ is proper: the inverse image of each compact subset of $[0,\infty)$ is compact.

Let $a\le b$ and $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]). The function $f$ is
**absolutely continuous** on $[a,b]$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$\delta>0$ such that every finite family of subintervals
$[u_j,v_j]\subseteq[a,b]$, indexed by $j<m$, whose open interiors are pairwise
disjoint and which satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}(v_j-u_j)<\delta$$

also satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}|f(v_j)-f(u_j)|<\varepsilon.$$

Finite sums and the empty sum are those of [[def-finite-sum]] and
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. For $m=0$ both sums are $0$, so the condition is
automatic. On $[a,a]$ every permitted interval is a singleton and every endpoint
increment is $0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), so every function on that singleton is
absolutely continuous. Absolute continuity implies ordinary continuity
([[def-continuity-real]]); that implication is proved next rather than built into
the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $F\in AC[a,b]$, then $F'$ exists almost everywhere on $(a,b)$ and belongs to
$L^1[a,b]$.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the causal-curve class of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]].

**(a) Chart independence.** Local absolute continuity in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (a) is independent of the
chosen chart and of the smooth atlas. Every compact parameter interval
admits a finite subdivision on each of whose pieces a chart representative
is absolutely continuous. For a continuous curve, the relative neighborhood
formulation and the compact chart-interval formulation of that definition
are equivalent.

**(b) Velocity and smooth composition.** At every interior parameter value
$t$ at which one chart representative is differentiable, every chart
representative is differentiable, the velocity $\gamma'(t)$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (b) is well defined and
independent of the chart, and the set of parameter values at which some
chart representative is differentiable has full measure in the domain. For
every smooth map $F$ of an open subset of $M$ into a finite-dimensional
smooth manifold $P$ (in particular $P=\mathbb R$) whose domain contains
the image of $\gamma$, the composite $F\circ\gamma$ is locally absolutely
continuous in charts of $P$ using the same relative neighborhood definition,
and $(F\circ\gamma)'(t)=dF_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t))$ at almost
every parameter value $t$.

**(c) Piecewise $C^1$ curves.** Every piecewise $C^1$ curve (with the finite
admissible partition and one-sided endpoint convention of clause (a) of
[[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]) is locally absolutely
continuous; a piecewise $C^1$ curve all of whose tangents are future causal
is a future causal curve, and if in addition its tangents are future
timelike, it is a future timelike curve.

**(d) Concatenation.** If $\gamma_1:[a,b]\to M$ and $\gamma_2:[b,c]\to M$ are
future causal curves (respectively future timelike curves) with
$\gamma_1(b)=\gamma_2(b)$, then the concatenation $\gamma:[a,c]\to M$,
$\gamma(t):=\gamma_1(t)$ for $t\le b$ and $\gamma(t):=\gamma_2(t)$ for
$t\ge b$, is a future causal (respectively future timelike) curve; the same
holds for any finite chain of such curves.

**(e) Reparametrization.** If $\varphi:J\to I$ is a strictly increasing
$C^1$ diffeomorphism of intervals with $\varphi'>0$ and $\gamma:I\to M$ is
locally absolutely continuous, then $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is locally
absolutely continuous and $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is future causal (respectively
future timelike) exactly when $\gamma$ is. Moreover $\gamma$ is
future-inextendible if and only if $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is
future-inextendible, and this equivalence holds for every strictly increasing
continuous surjection $\varphi$ of intervals, not only the $C^1$ ones.

**(f) Relations.** The relation $\le$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] is reflexive and transitive, and
$p\ll q$ implies $p\le q$ for all $p,q$; the relations $J^{\pm}$ and
$I^{\pm}$ of that definition are therefore nested, $I^{\pm}(S)\subseteq
J^{\pm}(S)$ for every $S\subseteq M$.

On a connected Riemannian manifold define $d_g(p,q)=\inf\{L_g(\gamma):\gamma\text{ is piecewise }C^1\text{ from }p\text{ to }q\}$.

Lengths are those of [[def-riemannian-speed-and-length]]. For each pair $p,q$, [[lem-any-two-points-in-a-connected-smooth-manifold-can-be-joined-by-a-piecewise-c-one-curve]] supplies a curve, so the set of lengths is nonempty, contains a finite real number and is bounded below by zero. Applying the least-upper-bound property [[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]] to the negatives gives a finite nonnegative infimum. On the empty connected manifold this defines the empty distance function; there are no pairs to evaluate. No minimizing curve is part of this definition.
$d_g$ is a finite metric on a connected Riemannian manifold.
The topology of $d_g$ is the manifold topology on every connected Riemannian manifold.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g)$ be a **nonempty**, connected,
boundaryless Riemannian manifold, and let $d=d_g$ be its Riemannian distance.
The following conditions are equivalent.

1. The metric space $(M,d)$ is complete.
2. The Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ is geodesically complete.
3. For every $p\in M$, the fibre exponential domain is all of the tangent
   space: $\mathcal E_p=T_pM$.
4. There is a point $p_0\in M$ for which $\mathcal E_{p_0}=T_{p_0}M$.
5. Every closed bounded subset of the metric space $(M,d)$ is compact.

Whenever these conditions hold, every $x,y\in M$ are joined by a minimizing
geodesic. More exactly, there is $v\in T_xM$ with
$$
\exp_x(v)=y,\qquad |v|_{g_x}=d(x,y),
$$
and $t\mapsto\exp_x(tv)$ on $[0,1]$ has length $d(x,y)$.

The nonemptiness hypothesis is essential for this formulation: on the empty
manifold conditions 1--3 and 5 are vacuous, whereas condition 4 is false.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{T}_d$ be
its metric topology ([[def-metric-topology]]), so that $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$ is a
topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and is metrizable
([[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. $(X,d)$ is a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]) **if and only
   if** $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$ is a compact topological space
   ([[def-compact-space]]).
2. For every $A \subseteq X$: $A$ is a compact subset of the metric space
   $(X,d)$ if and only if $A$ is a compact subset of the topological space
   $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$, the two readings of "compact subset" being the metric
   subspace $(A, d_A)$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]) and the topological
   subspace $(A, (\mathcal{T}_d)_A)$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Nothing here is a coincidence and nothing is transported.** The open-cover
condition of [[def-metric-compactness]] quantifies over families of subsets open
in $(X,d)$, and by [[def-metric-topology]] those are exactly the members of
$\mathcal{T}_d$; so the two conditions are not merely equivalent, they are the
same condition written twice. No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with compactness as in
[[def-metric-compactness]] and the three variants as in
[[def-metric-compactness-variants]]. Then:

1. If $(X,d)$ is compact, it is countably compact.
2. If $(X,d)$ is compact, it is limit point compact.
3. If $(X,d)$ is countably compact, it is sequentially compact.
4. If $(X,d)$ is limit point compact, it is sequentially compact.

**Every one of the four is a theorem of ZF.** Where a subsequence is extracted,
the index at each stage is the **least** admissible one, which
[[thm-well-ordering-principle]] makes canonical and [[thm-recursion]] then
assembles into a function; where finitely many indices have to be recovered from
finitely many sets, [[lem-finite-choice]] supplies them and is itself a theorem
of ZF. Nothing below appeals to countable or to dependent choice.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $(x_k)$ be a Cauchy
sequence in $X$ ([[def-cauchy-in-metric]]), and suppose some subsequence
$(x_{n_j})$ converges to $p \in X$, that is $p$ is a subsequential limit of
$(x_k)$ in $(X,d)$ ([[def-metric-convergence]], [[def-subsequential-limit]]).
Then the whole sequence converges to $p$.

In particular a Cauchy sequence has at most one subsequential limit, and it has
one exactly when it converges.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, and let $n$ be an observer at $p$
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]). Write $h:=h_n$,
$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,n)=0\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]) and
$\mathbb Rn=\{\lambda n:\lambda\in\mathbb R\}$. Then:

1. $h:T_pM\to T_pM$ is linear, $h(n)=0$, $h(v)=v$ for every $v\in n^{\perp}$
   and $h\circ h=h$; its kernel is $\ker h=\mathbb Rn$, its image is
   $\operatorname{im}h=n^{\perp}$, and
   $T_pM=\mathbb Rn\oplus n^{\perp}$ is an orthogonal direct sum: every
   $v\in T_pM$ has the unique decomposition

   $$v=-g_p(v,n)\,n+h(v),$$

   in which $-g_p(v,n)n\in\mathbb Rn$ and $h(v)\in n^{\perp}$.
2. For all $v,w\in T_pM$ the **projection identity**

   $$g_p(h(v),h(w))=g_p(v,w)+g_p(v,n)g_p(n,w)$$

   holds; in particular $g_p(h(v),h(v))=g_p(v,v)+g_p(v,n)^2$.
3. $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive
   definite.

derivations.claim: (Clause (a).) Let $q\in M$ and $v\in T_qM$ nonzero, and decompose $v=\alpha n_q+w$ as in [L2]. Then $g_q(v,n_q)=-\alpha$, so $$h_q(v,v)=g_q(v,v)+2g_q(v,n_q)^2=-\alpha^2+g_q(w,w)+2\alpha^2=\alpha^2+g_q(w,w).$$ If $w\ne0$ then $g_q(w,w)>0$ by positive definiteness on $n_q^\perp$, so $h_q(v,v)>0$; if $w=0$ then $\alpha\ne0$ and $h_q(v,v)=\alpha^2>0$. Symmetry of $h$ is inherited from $g$ and the symmetric product $n^\flat\otimes n^\flat$, and smoothness from [L1]. This proves (a).

(Length and the distance for locally absolutely continuous curves.) Let $M_0$ be a connected component, let $H$ be a smooth Riemannian metric on it, and let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M_0$ be locally absolutely continuous. Its image is compact, so subdivide $[a,b]$ into finitely many pieces whose coordinate images lie in convex chart balls with compact closure. On each piece the smooth metric coefficients are bounded and the coordinate derivative is integrable; hence the integrand defining $\ell_H$ is measurable and dominated by a constant times the Euclidean coordinate speed, so $\ell_H(\gamma)<\infty$. Fix $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$. Refine the subdivision so that on each piece the metric matrix differs from a fixed positive form $H_i$ by relative bounds $(1-\varepsilon)H_i\le H\le(1+\varepsilon)H_i$, which is possible by continuity and compactness. For the coordinate endpoints $x_i,x_{i+1}$ of a piece, the straight coordinate segment stays in its convex chart ball and has $H$-length at most $\sqrt{1+\varepsilon}\,|x_{i+1}-x_i|_{H_i}$. Since $x_{i+1}-x_i=\int x'(t)\,dt$, the triangle inequality for the norm induced by $H_i$ gives
$$|x_{i+1}-x_i|_{H_i}\le\int |x'(t)|_{H_i}\,dt\le(1-\varepsilon)^{-1/2}\int\sqrt{H_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t))}\,dt.$$
The distance between the piece endpoints is no larger than the length of this piecewise-$C^1$ segment. Summing over pieces and using the triangle inequality for $d_H$ gives $d_H(\gamma(a),\gamma(b))\le\sqrt{(1+\varepsilon)/(1-\varepsilon)}\,\ell_H(\gamma)$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves the asserted inequality.

(The conformal factor.) By [L4] choose a smooth nonnegative proper $f$ and set $h':=(1+|df|_h^2)h$. By [L3], applied at each point with $H=h$, the field $h'$ is positive definite and smooth and satisfies $|df|_{h'}\le1$ everywhere. This proves (b).

(The proper function is $1$-Lipschitz for $h'$.) Let $q,q'\in M_0$ and let $\varepsilon>0$. By [[def-riemannian-distance-on-a-connected-manifold]], choose a piecewise-$C^1$ curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M_0$ from $q$ to $q'$ whose $h'$-length is at most $d_{h'}(q,q')+\varepsilon$. On each smooth piece, [L5] and Cauchy--Schwarz give $|f(\gamma(v))-f(\gamma(u))|\le\int_u^v |df|_{h'}\,|\gamma'|_{h'}\,dt\le L_{h'}(\gamma|_{[u,v]})$. Summing over the finitely many pieces yields $|f(q')-f(q)|\le L_{h'}(\gamma)\le d_{h'}(q,q')+\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ gives $|f(q')-f(q)|\le d_{h'}(q,q')$.

(Completeness.) Let $(x_k)$ be a Cauchy sequence in $(M_0,d_{h'})$. There is $k_0$ with $d_{h'}(x_k,x_{k_0})\le1$ for all $k\ge k_0$; by step 3.1, $f(x_k)\le f(x_{k_0})+1$ for those $k$, so the tail lies in the closed sublevel $K:=f^{-1}\bigl([0,f(x_{k_0})+1]\bigr)$. The set $K$ is compact in $M$ by [L4]. Every connected component is closed (the closure of a connected set is connected), so $K_0:=K\cap M_0$ is compact in $M_0$ and contains the tail. By [L7] that tail has a subsequence converging in $K_0$; the limit is a manifold-topology limit and therefore a $d_{h'}$-limit by [L6]. Since $(x_k)$ is Cauchy, the whole sequence converges to the same limit. Hence $(M_0,d_{h'})$ is complete, which is (c).

(Clause (d).) Apply [L8] to the connected Riemannian manifold $(M_0,h'|_{M_0})$, which is complete by step 4.1: every closed $d_{h'}$-bounded subset of $M_0$ is compact, and every closed ball is compact. This proves (d).
(Conclusion.) Steps 1.1-5.1 prove (a)-(d), and step 1.2 establishes the locally absolutely continuous length convention stated above.

boundaries.reason: The pointwise metric claim is vacuous on an empty manifold; componentwise distance and completeness conclusions quantify only over components actually present.

boundaries.evidence: df=0 is allowed: step 2.1 then has conformal factor 1 and norm zero, so no division by df occurs. N has strictly negative Lorentz norm before normalization.
Statement boundary: For a closed radius-zero distance ball, metric definiteness gives the singleton centre; componentwise compactness includes that set.
Step 1.1 separates w=0 from w nonzero in v=alpha*n+w, proving positivity for both allowed types of nonzero tangent.

boundaries.reason: The construction has no finite time boundary; completeness concerns arbitrary Cauchy sequences in each connected component.

boundaries.evidence: Countable Choice is declared for the proper smooth function supplier. The distance estimate in step 3.1 chooses one curve within epsilon of the infimum, not a global minimizing family.

boundaries.reason: The theorem constructs h and h-prime and proves their properties; completeness is a consequence, not a biconditional hypothesis.
No claim says every complete metric arises by this conformal proper-function construction.

risk_review.notes: Checked positivity via rest-space decomposition, conformal inverse scaling, proper sublevels intersected with closed components, and Hopf-Rinow. Length comparison by finite chart segments is sound under AC_omega/DC; added the missing DC qualifier only to that assertion. Direct users of the AC inequality already declare DC; the AC_omega-only geodesic-extension remark uses only completeness, whose hypotheses are unchanged. Reader repair amended, confidence 1.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the
causal curves and the relations $\le$, $\ll$, $I^{\pm}$, $J^{\pm}$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]. All curves below are curves in
that sense.

**(a) Chronology and causality.** $(M,g,N)$ is **chronological** when there is
no $p\in M$ with $p\ll p$, equivalently when there is no nonconstant future
timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$. It is **causal**
when there is no nonconstant future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with
$\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$; a nonconstant future causal curve with equal endpoints
is called a **closed causal curve**, and a closed future timelike curve is
called a **closed timelike curve**.

**(b) Strong causality.** $(M,g,N)$ is **strongly causal** when for every
$p\in M$ and every open set $U\subseteq M$ with $p\in U$ there is an open set
$V$ with $p\in V\subseteq U$ such that for every future causal curve
$\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ and all $a\le s<t\le b$ with $\gamma(s)\in V$ and
$\gamma(t)\in V$ one has $\gamma([s,t])\subseteq V$. Thus no causal curve can
leave $V$ and later re-enter it; a set $V$ with this property for all causal
curves is called **causally convex for causal curves that meet it twice**.

**(c) Global hyperbolicity.** $(M,g,N)$ is **globally hyperbolic** when it is
strongly causal and for all $p,q\in M$ the **causal diamond**
$J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ is compact in the subspace topology
([[def-compact-space]]).

**(d) Time functions.** A **time function** on $(M,g,N)$ is a function
$u:M\to\mathbb R$ which is continuous from the manifold topology to the usual topology of
$\mathbb R$: for every $p\in M$ and every open neighborhood $W$ of $u(p)$
there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $p$ with $u(V)\subseteq W$
([[def-continuous-map-top]]). It also satisfies
$u(\gamma(a))<u(\gamma(b))$ for every future causal curve
$\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $a<b$ that is not constant on $[a,b]$.

**(e) Temporal functions.** A **temporal function** on $(M,g,N)$ is a smooth
function $u:M\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]])
whose gradient is past-directed timelike: writing $du$ for its differential
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]) and $\nabla u$ for the vector field
with $g(\nabla u,X)=du(X)$ for every smooth vector field $X$, constructed from
the inverse metric of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]], one
has
$$g(\nabla u,\nabla u)<0\qquad\text{and}\qquad du(N)=g(\nabla u,N)>0 .$$
The first inequality says that the gradient is nowhere zero and timelike; the
second fixes it as past-directed for the chosen time orientation. No level set
of a temporal function is asserted here to be a hypersurface or to be
spacelike, and no relation between temporal functions and compactness is
asserted; those claims are proved separately where they are used.

**(f) Scope and conventions.** These are mathematical conditions on the
Lorentzian model. Different sources define global hyperbolicity by equivalent
but differently phrased conditions; this page fixes the formulation of (c)
and proves the implications it uses. In particular no equivalence between
global hyperbolicity and the existence of a Cauchy hypersurface is asserted
by this definition, and the physical reading of strong causality or global
hyperbolicity as predictability of a classical model is adopted only in the
framework postulates.

For the absolutely continuous curve conclusion (c), assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]) as required by the cited causal-curve calculus and fundamental theorem. The other clauses use the given smooth observer structure, pointwise adapted-chart existence and finite compactness arguments, without these additional curve-calculus premises. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), and put $n=N/\sqrt{-g(N,N)}$. Write $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. In a chart $(U,x)$ put $v^a=dx^a(v)$, $v_s=(v^1,v^2,v^3)$ and $|v|_{\mathrm e}=(\sum_{a=0}^3(v^a)^2)^{1/2}$.

**(a) Adapted orthonormal charts.** For every $p\in M$ there are a chart $(U,x)$, $x(p)=0$, a radius $r>0$ with $U=x^{-1}(B_r)$, and $K\ge1$, such that on all of $U$
$$n=\partial_{x^0},\qquad g_{00}\equiv-1,\qquad g_{ab}(p)=\eta_{ab}.$$

**(b) Cone domination.** The chart and radius in (a) can be chosen so every nonzero future causal vector at any point of $U$ satisfies
$$|v_s|\le K v^0,\qquad |v^i|\le K v^0\quad(i=1,2,3),\qquad v^0\ge K^{-1}|v|_{\mathrm e}>0.$$

**(c) Curve form.** Every future causal curve $\gamma:I\to U$ of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] has strictly increasing time coordinate, and for all $s<t$ in $I$
$$x^0(\gamma(s))<x^0(\gamma(t)),\qquad |x_s(\gamma(t))-x_s(\gamma(s))|\le K\left(x^0(\gamma(t))-x^0(\gamma(s))\right).$$
Consequently every spatial component satisfies the same bound, and the curve image is the graph of a $K$-Lipschitz function into Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$ over the interval $x^0(\gamma(I))$.

**(d) Flat minorant cone.** The same chart can be chosen so the constant-coordinate metric $\eta_{16}=-(dx^0)^2+16\sum_i(dx^i)^2$ has every nonzero $\eta_{16}$-causal vector $g$-timelike throughout $U$. If $q,q'\in U$ and $\eta_{16}(x(q')-x(q),x(q')-x(q))<0$, then $q\ll q'$ if $x^0(q')>x^0(q)$, and $q'\ll q$ otherwise.

**(e) General temporal charts: exact compact uniformity.** For any chart $(U',z)$ define its temporal locus
$$P=\{q\in U':\nabla z^0(q)\text{ is past timelike}\}.$$
For every compact set $K_0\subset P$ there is $L\ge1$ such that all nonzero future causal vectors based in $K_0$, with coordinate components and Euclidean norm taken in $z$, satisfy
$$|v_s|\le L v^0,\qquad |v^i|\le L v^0,\qquad v^0\ge L^{-1}|v|_{\mathrm e}>0.$$
In particular these bounds hold throughout any relatively compact $U_0\Subset U'$ whose closure is contained in $P$, equivalently whose time gradient is past timelike on its entire closure. Timelikeness merely on $U_0$ gives local bounds at each point and uniform bounds on each compact subset of $U_0$; it does not alone give a uniform bound on all of $U_0$.

No additional choice is used to select the pointwise linear bases or compact cone constants. Countable and Dependent Choice are explicitly required only for the general absolutely continuous curve clause (c), through its actual calculus suppliers.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian
four-manifold ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and put
$$n:=\frac{N}{\sqrt{-g(N,N)}}\quad\text{(pointwise)},\qquad h:=g+2\,n^\flat\otimes n^\flat,$$
with the flat map $\flat$ of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],
so that $h$ is a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Then:

For each connected component $M_0\subseteq M$ and smooth Riemannian metric
$H$, let $d_H$ denote the Riemannian distance of $H|_{M_0}$. For the following absolutely continuous length assertion, also assume
Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]), as required by the cited
fundamental theorem. For any locally
absolutely continuous curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M_0$, use the length
$$\ell_H(\gamma):=\int_a^b\sqrt{H_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t))}\,dt,$$
with the Lebesgue integral and almost-everywhere derivative. This extends the
piecewise-$C^1$ length of [[def-riemannian-speed-and-length]]. The distance
from [[def-riemannian-distance-on-a-connected-manifold]] satisfies
$d_H(\gamma(a),\gamma(b))\le\ell_H(\gamma)$; the proof is included below.

**(a)** $h$ is a smooth Riemannian (positive definite) metric on $M$.

**(b)** There is a smooth nonnegative proper function $f:M\to[0,\infty)$ such
that the metric
$$h':=(1+|df|_h^2)\,h$$
is a smooth Riemannian metric with $|df|_{h'}\le1$ everywhere.

**(c)** For each connected component $M_0$ of $M$, the metric space
$(M_0,d_{h'})$ is complete, where $d_{h'}$ is the Riemannian distance of
$h'|_{M_0}$ ([[def-riemannian-distance-on-a-connected-manifold]],
[[thm-riemannian-distance-is-a-metric]]).

**(d)** Consequently, for every connected component $M_0$, every subset of
$M_0$ that is closed in $M_0$ and bounded in $d_{h'}$ is compact, and every
closed ball $\{q\in M_0:d_{h'}(q,p)\le r\}$ is compact.

Let $a\le b$ and $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]). The function $f$ is
**absolutely continuous** on $[a,b]$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$\delta>0$ such that every finite family of subintervals
$[u_j,v_j]\subseteq[a,b]$, indexed by $j<m$, whose open interiors are pairwise
disjoint and which satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}(v_j-u_j)<\delta$$

also satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}|f(v_j)-f(u_j)|<\varepsilon.$$

Finite sums and the empty sum are those of [[def-finite-sum]] and
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. For $m=0$ both sums are $0$, so the condition is
automatic. On $[a,a]$ every permitted interval is a singleton and every endpoint
increment is $0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), so every function on that singleton is
absolutely continuous. Absolute continuity implies ordinary continuity
([[def-continuity-real]]); that implication is proved next rather than built into
the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $F\in AC[a,b]$, then $F'$ exists almost everywhere on $(a,b)$ and belongs to
$L^1[a,b]$.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

derivations.claim: (A finite precompact causally convex cover.) For each point of $K$, choose an adapted chart and a closed coordinate ball compactly contained in it. Use its open half-radius ball as the neighborhood in strong causality [L1], obtaining a causally convex open $V$ around the point contained in that smaller ball. The collection of all such admissible $V$, charts and radii covers $K$; compactness selects finitely many members, with no choice of a family indexed by all points of $K$. Write them $V_j\subset U_j$ for $1\le j\le m$, with $U_j$ their open coordinate balls and $\overline{U_j}$ compactly contained in their respective larger charts. Define $M_j=\sup_{U_j}x_j^0-\inf_{U_j}x_j^0<\infty$, $H_j=\max_{\overline{U_j}}\|h\|_{\mathrm e,\mathrm{op}}<\infty$, and $c_j=\max\{1,\sqrt{H_j}K_j\}$. Then [L2] gives $\sqrt{h(\gamma',\gamma')}\le c_j(x_j^0\circ\gamma)'$ almost everywhere on every subarc in $U_j$. If $K$ is empty the conclusion is immediate with $L(K)=0$; henceforth use the finite cover for nonempty $K$.

(The visit of a causal curve to one causally convex set is one interval.) Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to K$ be future causal and fix $j$. If $s<t$ with $\gamma(s),\gamma(t)\in V_j$, then $\gamma([s,t])\subseteq V_j$ by the defining property of $V_j$; hence the parameter set $\gamma^{-1}(V_j)$ is an interval in $[a,b]$: whenever it contains $s<t$ it contains $[s,t]$. In particular $\gamma^{-1}(V_j)$ has at most one connected component and is an interval $I_j$, possibly empty.

(Length over a compact part of one visit.) For every compact nondegenerate $[s,t]\subset I_j$, the curve image lies in $V_j\subset U_j$, so the fundamental theorem in [L4] and step 1.1 give $\int_s^t\sqrt{h(\gamma',\gamma')}\le c_j\int_s^t(x_j^0\circ\gamma)'=c_j(x_j^0(\gamma(t))-x_j^0(\gamma(s)))\le c_jM_j$. The restricted speed is integrable, since the coordinate derivatives are integrable and dominate it. The relatively open visit $I_j=\gamma^{-1}(V_j)$ need not contain its endpoints; only compact subintervals contained in $I_j$ are used in this argument.

(Finite compact-interval cover and length sum.) The relatively open intervals $I_j$ form a finite cover of the compact parameter interval $[a,b]$. A sufficiently fine finite partition has each of its closed subintervals contained in some $I_j$, by a Lebesgue number of this cover. Assign each partition piece to the least such $j$; this requires only finitely many choices. For every index used, let $J_j$ be the closed interval from the least left endpoint to the greatest right endpoint of its assigned pieces. As $I_j$ is an interval, $J_j\subset I_j$; these finitely many compact intervals cover $[a,b]$. Step 3.1 applies on each $J_j$. The nonnegative integral over their union is at most the sum of their integrals, so the global speed is integrable and $\ell_h(\gamma)\le\sum_j\int_{J_j}\sqrt{h(\gamma',\gamma')}\le\sum_{j=1}^m c_jM_j=:L(K)<\infty$, with unused indices contributing no interval. If $a=b$ the length is zero. For an arclength-parametrized curve $\ell_h(\gamma)=b-a$, giving the second assertion. No possibly missing visit endpoint is evaluated.

(Imprisonment form.) There is no sequence of future causal curves with images in a fixed compact $K$ and auxiliary lengths tending to infinity: each length is bounded by the same $L(K)$ from step 4.1. Equivalently, there is no family of $h$-arclength-parametrized future causal curves with images in $K$ and parameter-domain lengths tending to infinity.
(Conclusion.) The finite causally convex cover, the interval visit estimate and the nonnegative integral bound establish both assertions, with exactly the declared calculus premises.

boundaries.evidence: step 2.1 treats the empty case explicitly.
Step 4.1 assigns zero length when a=b; the local constants c_j are at least 1, avoiding division by a vanishing speed.
One selected causally convex neighborhood gives L(K)=c_1*M_1; the interval visit argument in step 2.1 needs no second cover member.

boundaries.reason: The auxiliary metric is positive definite and the spacetime strongly causal; singular h or a causal-loop compact trap is outside the hypotheses.

boundaries.evidence: Step 3.1 integrates only closed subintervals contained in each visit I_j; step 4.1 never evaluates a missing open-visit endpoint.
The cover consists of all admissible chart/neighborhood tuples; compactness picks finitely many in step 1.1, and step 4.1 assigns each partition piece to the least available index.

boundaries.reason: The bounded-length assertion follows from strong causality; the imprisonment restatement in step 5.1 is the same bound expressed for lengths tending to infinity.
No converse from the bounded length of one compact set to strong causality of the spacetime is claimed.

risk_review.notes: Checked causally convex V_j within precompact cone charts. Each visit preimage is one relatively open interval. A Lebesgue-number partition groups pieces into closed hulls contained in visits; nonnegative integrals give the finite sum bound without evaluating missing visit endpoints. Empty K and zero length handled; DC explicit. Reader repair accepted.
