Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(a) Observers.** An **observer at $p$** is a tangent vector
$n\in T_pM$ such that $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ is future-directed in the sense of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], that is, $g_p(n,N_p)<0$. Because
$g_p(n,n)=-1\neq0$, an observer is timelike and in particular nonzero
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). Observers at $p$ exist:
the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and
$n:=N_p/\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}$ satisfies $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and
$g_p(n,N_p)=-\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}<0$, where the square root is the
nonnegative root of [[def-rational-power]]; then $-n$ is a unit timelike
vector with $g_p(-n,N_p)>0$, so it is not an observer, and the two vectors
$n,-n$ point in opposite time directions.

**(b) Rest space.** For an observer $n$ at $p$, the **rest space** of $n$ is
the $g_p$-orthogonal complement of the line $\mathbb Rn$,

$$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM: g_p(v,n)=0\},$$

in the sense of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. It is
a linear subspace of $T_pM$. The further facts that $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and
that the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive definite are proved
in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]; they are consequences, not
part of the definition.

**(c) Spatial projection.** The **spatial projection** of the observer $n$ is
the map

$$h_n:T_pM\longrightarrow T_pM,\qquad h_n(v):=v+g_p(n,v)\,n .$$

The map is linear because $g_p$ is bilinear, its image is contained in
$n^{\perp}$, and it fixes $n^{\perp}$ pointwise; that it is the
$g_p$-orthogonal projection onto $n^{\perp}$ with kernel $\mathbb Rn$ is
proved in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]].

**(d) Scope.** An observer at $p$ is a single tangent vector. It is not an
ordered basis or frame of $T_pM$, not a chart, not a field of observers such as
the congruences defined later on this page, and not a curve or a worldline: no
parametrized curve, clock reading, proper time or measurement is attached to
$n$ by this definition. The physical reading of an observer as the direction
of an ideal clock's worldline, and the measurement interpretation of the
observer-relative quantities introduced later on this page, belong to the
physical postulates and unit conventions of the framework and are not asserted
here.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal
classification of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and the
equivalence of "future-directed" with "pairing negatively with $N$" supplied by
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a continuous map,
where $I$ has its relative topology. A **chart representative** on a parameter
neighborhood $J\subseteq I$ is $x\circ\gamma|_J$, where $(U,x)$ is a smooth
chart and $\gamma(J)\subseteq U$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for each $t\in I$ there are
$\delta>0$ and a chart $(U,x)$ such that
$\gamma(I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta))\subseteq U$ and every coordinate of
$x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of
$I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta)$ in the sense of
[[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]. This includes one-sided neighborhoods
at included endpoints. Equivalently, for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the coordinates of $x\circ\gamma$ are
absolutely continuous on $[a,b]$. The equivalence and independence of the
chart and smooth atlas are proved in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]]
clause (a); continuity is part of both formulations.

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point: a
constant chart representative has derivative zero everywhere in its interior,
contradicting the full-measure nonzero-velocity requirement.

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ q\in J^+(p)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the causal-curve class of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]].

**(a) Chart independence.** Local absolute continuity in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (a) is independent of the
chosen chart and of the smooth atlas. Every compact parameter interval
admits a finite subdivision on each of whose pieces a chart representative
is absolutely continuous. For a continuous curve, the relative neighborhood
formulation and the compact chart-interval formulation of that definition
are equivalent.

**(b) Velocity and smooth composition.** At every interior parameter value
$t$ at which one chart representative is differentiable, every chart
representative is differentiable, the velocity $\gamma'(t)$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (b) is well defined and
independent of the chart, and the set of parameter values at which some
chart representative is differentiable has full measure in the domain. For
every smooth map $F$ of an open subset of $M$ into a finite-dimensional
smooth manifold $P$ (in particular $P=\mathbb R$) whose domain contains
the image of $\gamma$, the composite $F\circ\gamma$ is locally absolutely
continuous in charts of $P$ using the same relative neighborhood definition,
and $(F\circ\gamma)'(t)=dF_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t))$ at almost
every parameter value $t$.

**(c) Piecewise $C^1$ curves.** Every piecewise $C^1$ curve (with the finite
admissible partition and one-sided endpoint convention of clause (a) of
[[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]) is locally absolutely
continuous; a piecewise $C^1$ curve all of whose tangents are future causal
is a future causal curve, and if in addition its tangents are future
timelike, it is a future timelike curve.

**(d) Concatenation.** If $\gamma_1:[a,b]\to M$ and $\gamma_2:[b,c]\to M$ are
future causal curves (respectively future timelike curves) with
$\gamma_1(b)=\gamma_2(b)$, then the concatenation $\gamma:[a,c]\to M$,
$\gamma(t):=\gamma_1(t)$ for $t\le b$ and $\gamma(t):=\gamma_2(t)$ for
$t\ge b$, is a future causal (respectively future timelike) curve; the same
holds for any finite chain of such curves.

**(e) Reparametrization.** If $\varphi:J\to I$ is a strictly increasing
$C^1$ diffeomorphism of intervals with $\varphi'>0$ and $\gamma:I\to M$ is
locally absolutely continuous, then $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is locally
absolutely continuous and $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is future causal (respectively
future timelike) exactly when $\gamma$ is. Moreover $\gamma$ is
future-inextendible if and only if $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is
future-inextendible, and this equivalence holds for every strictly increasing
continuous surjection $\varphi$ of intervals, not only the $C^1$ ones.

**(f) Relations.** The relation $\le$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] is reflexive and transitive, and
$p\ll q$ implies $p\le q$ for all $p,q$; the relations $J^{\pm}$ and
$I^{\pm}$ of that definition are therefore nested, $I^{\pm}(S)\subseteq
J^{\pm}(S)$ for every $S\subseteq M$.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, and let $n$ be an observer at $p$
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]). For $w\in T_pM$ write
$h=h_n$ and $\gamma(w):=-g_p(n,w)$.

1. If $w$ is nonzero future causal, then $\gamma(w)>0$.
2. If $w$ is future unit timelike, then $\gamma(w)\ge1$, with
   $\gamma(w)=1$ if and only if $w=n$, and
   $g_p(h(w),h(w))=\gamma(w)^2-1$.
3. If $w$ is unit timelike, then $w$ is future-directed if and only if
   $g_p(n,w)<0$, and past-directed if and only if $g_p(n,w)>0$; in particular
   $g_p(n,w)\neq0$ for such $w$.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $M$ be a topological $n$-manifold and let $p\in M$. For every open
neighbourhood $O$ of $p$ there is a chart $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and an
open Euclidean ball $B(c,r)\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that

$$p\in \varphi^{-1}[B(c,r)]\subseteq O,\qquad \overline{B(c,r)}\subseteq \varphi(U).$$

Consequently the sets $\varphi^{-1}[B(c,r)]$ of this form constitute a basis of
the topology of $M$. Their closures in $M$ are compact.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal
classification of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and the
equivalence of "future-directed" with "pairing negatively with $N$" supplied by
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a continuous map,
where $I$ has its relative topology. A **chart representative** on a parameter
neighborhood $J\subseteq I$ is $x\circ\gamma|_J$, where $(U,x)$ is a smooth
chart and $\gamma(J)\subseteq U$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for each $t\in I$ there are
$\delta>0$ and a chart $(U,x)$ such that
$\gamma(I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta))\subseteq U$ and every coordinate of
$x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of
$I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta)$ in the sense of
[[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]. This includes one-sided neighborhoods
at included endpoints. Equivalently, for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the coordinates of $x\circ\gamma$ are
absolutely continuous on $[a,b]$. The equivalence and independence of the
chart and smooth atlas are proved in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]]
clause (a); continuity is part of both formulations.

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point: a
constant chart representative has derivative zero everywhere in its interior,
contradicting the full-measure nonzero-velocity requirement.

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ q\in J^+(p)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

derivations.claim: (A wider flat metric.) Fix the adapted chart $(U_0,x)$ and the constant $K$ of [L1]. Define $g_\varepsilon$ on $U_0$ with $\varepsilon:=3K^2$. For every $q\in U_0$ and every nonzero future $g$-causal $v\in T_qM$ one has $(v^0)^2>0$ and $\sum_{i=1}^3(v^i)^2\le3K^2(v^0)^2$, so $$g_\varepsilon(v,v)=-(1+\varepsilon)(v^0)^2+\sum_{i=1}^3(v^i)^2\le(3K^2-1-\varepsilon)(v^0)^2=-(v^0)^2<0,$$ and $v^0>0$: thus $v$ is future $g_\varepsilon$-timelike. Consequently every future $g$-causal curve whose velocity is nonzero almost everywhere is a future $g_\varepsilon$-timelike curve, and the same holds on every subinterval on which the velocity is nonzero almost everywhere.

(Explicit precompact diamonds.) Put $b_\varepsilon=\sqrt{1+\varepsilon}$ and choose $r>0$ so the closed coordinate ball $\overline{B_r(0)}$ lies in $x(U_0)$. Set $C=\sqrt{1+b_\varepsilon^2}$, fix $0<\delta_1<r/(2C)$, and define $\delta_k=\delta_1/k$, $r_k=x^{-1}(-\delta_k,0)$, $q_k=x^{-1}(\delta_k,0)$ and $V_k=x^{-1}(\{(\tau,z):|\tau|+|z|/b_\varepsilon<\delta_k\})$. Each $V_k$ is open, contains $p$, is contained in $x^{-1}(B_{C\delta_k})$, and has closure in the compact coordinate ball $x^{-1}(\overline{B_{C\delta_1}})\subset U_0\subset U$. They form a nested basis at $p$. These are exactly the flat chronological diamonds $I^+_\varepsilon(r_k)\cap I^-_\varepsilon(q_k)$ in $U_0$: the displayed strict inequalities yield the two straight future flat-timelike segments inside the coordinate ball; conversely, integrating a future flat-timelike velocity using the stated AC calculus gives $\Delta\tau>|\Delta z|/b_\varepsilon$ on a nondegenerate segment, which gives those inequalities for any point in the chronological intersection.

(Countable selection of witnesses.) For each $k\ge1$, the failure hypothesis on $V_k$ gives a nonempty set of witness tuples $(\sigma,s,t)$ with $s<t$, endpoints in $V_k$ and image of the restricted segment not contained in $V_k$. Countable Choice selects one tuple for every $k$. Restrict and reparametrize by the increasing affine map $u\mapsto s_k+u(t_k-s_k)$ to obtain a future causal curve $\sigma_k:[0,1]\to M$ whose endpoints are in $V_k$ and whose image is not contained in $V_k$. The affine map preserves AC directly by rescaling its defining modulus and preserves the full-measure velocity condition by a positive constant factor. This is the exact use of Countable Choice; no canonical witnesses were supplied by the failure hypothesis.

(Causal convexity relative to the chart.) For every $k$, $V_k$ is causally convex relative to $U_0$. Indeed, let $\lambda:[0,1]\to U_0$ be a future $g$-causal curve with endpoints in $V_k$. Step 1.1 makes it future $g_\varepsilon$-timelike. For each $u\in[0,1]$, concatenate the flat-timelike segment from $r_k$ to $\lambda(0)$, the restriction of $\lambda$ up to $u$, its restriction from $u$ onward, and the segment from $\lambda(1)$ to $q_k$ as appropriate. At $u=0$ or $1$ omit the degenerate restriction. Finite timelike concatenation gives $r_k\ll_\varepsilon\lambda(u)\ll_\varepsilon q_k$, so step 1.2 places $\lambda(u)$ in $V_k$. This proves the claimed relative convexity, and therefore also convexity of each smaller diamond relative to every larger one.

(Every witness escapes the fixed diamond.) If $\sigma_k([0,1])\subseteq V_1\subset U_0$, its endpoints in $V_k$ and step 2.1 would force its whole image into $V_k$, contradicting step 1.3. Thus $\sigma_k([0,1])\not\subseteq V_1$ for every $k\ge2$.

(Conclusions.) Take $W=V_1$, whose closure is contained in $U$ by step 1.2. For $k\ge2$ put $x_k=\sigma_k(0)$ and $y_k=\sigma_k(1)$. They are in $V_k\subset W$, and their coordinate norms are at most $C\delta_k\to0$, so both sequences converge to $p$. Step 3.1 proves every selected curve escapes $W$, as required.

boundaries.reason: The failure point p belongs to U and to the constructed diamonds V_k, so the neighborhoods and witness families are nonempty.

boundaries.evidence: Statement boundary: The limit diamond radius tends to zero as delta_1/k, but every finite-k radius is positive; epsilon=3K^2 is positive since K>=1.

boundaries.reason: An individual escape witness alone is insufficient; the claim requires a countably indexed sequence whose endpoints approach p.
Strong causality fails at the specified point; the theorem does not invoke a strong-causality assumption while constructing the witnesses.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.2 uses strict diamond inequalities and compact closures inside U; the selected curves escape W even though their endpoints remain inside it.
Step 1.3 names the nonempty witness tuples for each k and uses Countable Choice to select them; the AC curve-calculus suppliers also carry Dependent Choice.

boundaries.reason: The failure of strong causality is the hypothesis of this escape construction, with no reverse characterization asserted.
The existence of the listed endpoint sequences is not claimed here to establish the failure predicate in reverse.

risk_review.notes: Checked wider flat cone eps=3K^2, nested explicit diamonds, relative causal convexity and fixed-diamond escape. A witness contained in V_1 would stay in its own smaller V_k, contradiction. AC_omega chooses the fixed family of witnesses; AC calculus uses DC. Endpoints converge to p; no claim that shallow ball escape alone suffices.

citations.quote:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection, whose existence and uniqueness are
supplied by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; its
Christoffel symbols are the smooth chart functions of
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]. Recall that a **geodesic**
is a curve with $D_t\gamma'=0$ in its parameter
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]).

**(a) Local existence, uniqueness and maximality.** For every $(p,v)\in TM$
there is a unique maximal geodesic $\gamma_{p,v}:I_{p,v}\to M$ with
$\gamma_{p,v}(0)=p$ and $\gamma_{p,v}'(0)=v$; its domain $I_{p,v}$ is an open
interval containing $0$ and is not asserted to be all of $\mathbb R$.

**(b) Smooth dependence.** The set
$\mathcal G:=\{(t,p,v):t\in I_{p,v}\}\subseteq\mathbb R\times TM$ is open, and
the evaluation map $(t,p,v)\mapsto\gamma_{p,v}(t)$ is smooth on $\mathcal G$.

**(c) Scaling.** For every $s\in\mathbb R$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$,
$t\in I_{p,sv}$ if and only if $st\in I_{p,v}$, and then
$\gamma_{p,sv}(t)=\gamma_{p,v}(st)$.

**(d) The exponential map.** Define $\mathcal E_p:=\{v\in T_pM:1\in I_{p,v}\}$
and $\exp_p:\mathcal E_p\to M$, $\exp_p(v):=\gamma_{p,v}(1)$, and let
$\psi_p:T_pM\to\mathbb R^4$ be the coordinate isomorphism of a basis
$e_0,\dots,e_3$ of $T_pM$. Then $\mathcal E_p$ is open and star-shaped about
$0$ (if $v\in\mathcal E_p$ and $0\le s\le1$, then $sv\in\mathcal E_p$),
$\exp_p$ is smooth, $\exp_p(0)=p$, and, under the canonical identification
$T_0(T_pM)\cong T_pM$ induced by the chart $\psi_p$ on $T_pM$,
$$d(\exp_p)_0=\operatorname{id}_{T_pM}.$$
Consequently there is a star-shaped open neighborhood $W_p\subseteq\mathcal E_p$
of $0$ such that $\exp_p|_{W_p}$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of
$M$.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map and let $p\in M$. If $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ is
an isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $U$ of $p$ and $V$ of
$F(p)$ such that $F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism.

Let $F:M\to N$ be smooth and let $p\in M$. The **differential of $F$ at $p$** is the map $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ defined by
$$ dF_p(v)([g]):=v([g\circ F]) $$
for every derivation $v\in T_pM$ and every germ $[g]\in C_{F(p)}^\infty(N)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $M$ be a topological $n$-manifold and let $p\in M$. For every open
neighbourhood $O$ of $p$ there is a chart $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and an
open Euclidean ball $B(c,r)\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that

$$p\in \varphi^{-1}[B(c,r)]\subseteq O,\qquad \overline{B(c,r)}\subseteq \varphi(U).$$

Consequently the sets $\varphi^{-1}[B(c,r)]$ of this form constitute a basis of
the topology of $M$. Their closures in $M$ are compact.

derivations.claim: (Openness and smoothness of $\Phi$.) The set $\mathcal D=\{(q,v):(1,q,v)\in\mathcal G\}$ is the preimage of the open set $\mathcal G$ under the continuous map $(q,v)\mapsto(1,q,v)$; hence it is open in $TM$. The identity $\Phi(q,v)=(q,\gamma_{q,v}(1))$ exhibits $\Phi$ as the composition of the smooth map $(q,v)\mapsto(1,q,v)$ with the smooth evaluation of [L1] followed by the smooth map $(q,v)\mapsto(q,v)$; hence $\Phi$ is smooth, proving (a).

(Coordinate form of $\Phi$ and its differential.) Fix a chart $(U,x)$ around $p$, translate it so that $x(p)=0$, and write $TU\cong x(U)\times\mathbb R^4$, so that a tangent vector $v\in T_qM$ with $q\in U$ has components $\eta\in\mathbb R^4$. The coordinate representative of $\Phi$ is $$(\xi,\eta)\longmapsto\bigl(\xi,\ e(\xi,\eta)\bigr),\qquad e(\xi,\eta):=x\bigl(\exp_{x^{-1}(\xi)}(\eta)\bigr).$$ By [L1], $e$ is smooth on its domain, and $e(\xi,0)=\xi$ for every $\xi$, so $\partial e/\partial\xi(0,0)=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb R^4}$; and $\eta\mapsto e(0,\eta)=x(\exp_p(\eta))$ has derivative $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb R^4}$ at $\eta=0$ by the identity $d(\exp_p)_0=\operatorname{id}_{T_pM}$ of [L1] read in the chart. Therefore the Jacobian matrix of the representative at $(0,0)$ is the block matrix $\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\ I&I\end{pmatrix}$, i.e., in the identifications of (b) $$d\Phi_{(p,0)}(u,w)=(u,u+w).$$

(Invertibility and the diffeomorphism.) The map $(u,w)\mapsto(u,u+w)$ is an isomorphism with inverse $(u,y)\mapsto(u,y-u)$; hence $d\Phi_{(p,0)}$ is an isomorphism, and [L2] gives open neighborhoods $V_0$ of $(p,0)$ and $W_0$ of $(p,p)$ with $\Phi|_{V_0}:V_0\to W_0$ a diffeomorphism. In the bundle chart $(TU,Tx)$, the open neighborhood $V_0$ contains an exact product $x^{-1}(B_{r_0})\times B_{\rho_0}$ for some $r_0,\rho_0>0$, where the second factor records coordinate components of the tangent vector. Also, by [L5] in the product chart, $W_0$ contains $x^{-1}(B_{s_0})\times x^{-1}(B_{s_0})$ for some $s_0>0$.

(Product-like shape of $V$.) Take the exact product $V:=x^{-1}(B_r)\times B_\rho\subseteq V_0$ with $0<r<r_0$ and $0<\rho<\rho_0$, and set $W:=\Phi(V)$. Since $\Phi|_{V_0}$ is a diffeomorphism and $V$ is open, $W$ is open and contains $(p,p)$. By [L5], choose $s>0$ small enough that $x^{-1}(\overline{B_s})\times x^{-1}(\overline{B_s})\subseteq W$ and $s<r$. Then the open product is also contained in $W$. The set $V$ has exactly the displayed product-like form, and $\Phi|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. This proves the first two assertions of (c).

(The two-point inverse.) Define $v(q,r)$ for $(q,r)\in W$ as the second component of $\Phi^{-1}(q,r)\in V$. Since $\Phi^{-1}$ is smooth and the projection to the second factor is smooth, $v$ is smooth. The identity $\Phi(q,v(q,r))=(q,r)$ unwinds to $\exp_q(v(q,r))=r$ and $(q,v(q,r))\in V$. For $q=r$ we get $\exp_q(v(q,q))=q=\exp_q(0)$ with $(q,v(q,q)),(q,0)\in V$ and $\Phi(q,v(q,q))=\Phi(q,0)=(q,q)$, so $v(q,q)=0$ by injectivity of $\Phi|_V$. This proves the remaining assertions of (c).

(Lipschitz bound.) The closed product $x^{-1}(\overline{B_s})\times x^{-1}(\overline{B_s})$ is contained in $W$ by step 3.1. Let $M_0$ be the supremum of $\|Dv\|$ over its coordinate image $\overline{B_s}\times\overline{B_s}$, a compact convex set; it is finite because $v$ is smooth on the open set $W$. For fixed $q\in x^{-1}(B_s)$ and $r,r'\in x^{-1}(B_s)$, the straight coordinate segment from $x(r)$ to $x(r')$ lies in $B_s$, so [L4] applied to $t\mapsto v(q,x^{-1}(x(r)+t(x(r')-x(r))))$ gives $|v(q,r')-v(q,r)|_x\le M_0|x(r')-x(r)|_{\mathrm e}$. Taking $r=q$ and using $v(q,q)=0$ proves (d) with $\Lambda=M_0$; also $|x(q)-x(r)|_{\mathrm e}<2s$ gives $|v(q,r)|_x\le2\Lambda s$. This proves (d) and completes the proof.

boundaries.reason: The given p makes the joint domain nonempty because (p,0) has the constant geodesic defined at time 1.

boundaries.evidence: Statement boundary: Steps 1.2 and 4.1 explicitly handle zero velocity: the differential sends (u,w) to (u,u+w), and v(q,q)=0 follows from injectivity.
The fixed-base diagonal pair (p,p) is included in W, and the one-pair inverse identity is already proved in step 4.1.
Statement boundary: The block differential is invertible at (p,0); no inverse is taken at a singular differential outside the local inverse-function neighborhood.
Statement boundary: The time-1 evaluation is defined only on the open domain D with 1 in the maximal geodesic interval; no completeness of geodesics is asserted.

boundaries.reason: The inverse-function theorem supplies one neighborhood pair and positive radii; this local finite choice is not a choice function over every base point.
The local diffeomorphism and inverse bound are direct conclusions, not an equivalence between local and global injectivity.
No converse from a Lipschitz bound to existence of the exponential inverse is used.

risk_review.notes: Checked smooth evaluation domain, block derivative (u,u+w), inverse-function product restriction, smooth two-point inverse and compact derivative estimate. Amended c to require the closed product already selected in Step 3.1, making d uniform exactly where its proof applies. Existing consumers use sufficiently small selected products; their local existence inputs are strengthened, not lost. Confidence 1.

citations.quote:
In coordinates $x^1,\ldots,x^n$, a smooth curve $\gamma$ is a geodesic if and only if, throughout every parameter subinterval lying in the chart,
$$\ddot x^k+\Gamma^k{}_{ij}(x)\dot x^i\dot x^j=0\qquad(1\le k\le n),$$
with summation over repeated indices.

For an affine connection as in [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]] and coordinates $(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, its **Christoffel symbols** in this chart are the unique smooth functions $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ such that
$$\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\sum_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k.$$
The first lower index $i$ is the differentiating direction and the second lower index $j$ labels the differentiated vector field. In the coordinate frame, the one-forms from [[def-connection-one-form-in-a-local-frame]] are $\omega^k{}_j=\sum_i\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\,dx^i$. A different chart generally has different symbols. This definition asserts neither symmetry in $i,j$ nor tensorial transformation.

For dimension one there is one smooth coefficient $\Gamma^1{}_{11}$; in dimension zero there are no coefficients. All statements are local, and at a boundary chart the derivatives are the smooth up-to-boundary coordinate derivatives.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Since $0\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $C^0$ means continuity. The definitions also give $C^{k+1}\subseteq C^k$. Existence of $f^{(k)}$ alone does not assert that $f^{(k)}$ is continuous.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

For an affine connection as in [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]] and coordinates $(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, its **Christoffel symbols** in this chart are the unique smooth functions $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ such that
$$\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\sum_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k.$$
The first lower index $i$ is the differentiating direction and the second lower index $j$ labels the differentiated vector field. In the coordinate frame, the one-forms from [[def-connection-one-form-in-a-local-frame]] are $\omega^k{}_j=\sum_i\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\,dx^i$. A different chart generally has different symbols. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval ([[def-interval]]) and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$. For $x,y\in I$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$, the point $\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y$ belongs to $I$. The function $f$ is **convex** when the convex-combination inequality holds for every weight in $[0,1]$:

$$f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le \lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y).$$

It is **strictly convex** when this inequality is strict whenever $x\ne y$ and $0<\lambda<1$. It is **concave** (respectively **strictly concave**) when $-f$ is convex (respectively strictly convex). It is **midpoint convex** when the displayed inequality is required only at $\lambda=1/2$.

derivations.claim: (Computation of $f''$.) Write $x=x(\gamma(t))$, $\dot x=\dot x(t)$, $\ddot x=\ddot x(t)$ and $\Gamma=\Gamma(x(t))$. Since $f=|x|_{\mathrm e}^2=\sum_a(x^a)^2$, $$f'=2\sum_a x^a\dot x^a,\qquad f''=2\sum_a\bigl((\dot x^a)^2+x^a\ddot x^a\bigr)=2|\dot x|_{\mathrm e}^2+2\,x\cdot\ddot x .$$ By the geodesic equation of [L1], $\ddot x^a=-\sum_{i,j}\Gamma^a{}_{ij}\dot x^i\dot x^j$, so $f''=2|\dot x|_{\mathrm e}^2-2\,x\cdot\Gamma(x)[\dot x,\dot x]$.

(Bound.) By Cauchy–Schwarz in $\mathbb R^4$ and [L3], $\bigl|x\cdot\Gamma(x)[\dot x,\dot x]\bigr| \le|x|_{\mathrm e}\,\bigl|\Gamma(x)[\dot x,\dot x]\bigr|_{\mathrm e} \le|x|_{\mathrm e}\,\|\Gamma\|_K\,|\dot x|_{\mathrm e}^2$ whenever the image of $\gamma$ lies in $K$. Substituting into step 1.1 gives the displayed inequality, and if $x(K)\subseteq B_{r_1}$ with $\|\Gamma\|_K r_1\le\frac12$, then $f''\ge 2(1-\frac12)|\dot x|_{\mathrm e}^2=|\dot x|_{\mathrm e}^2\ge0$. This proves (a).

(Maximum principle.) Let $K$ and $r_2<r_1$ be as in (b), so the image of $\gamma$ lies in $K$ and $x(K)\subseteq B_{r_1}$ with $\|\Gamma\|_K r_1\le\frac12$. By step 2.1, $f''\ge0$ on the interval $[0,1]$; since $f$ is twice differentiable there by [L2], [L2] makes $f$ convex on $[0,1]$. By [L4], $f(t)\le\max\{f(0),f(1)\}\le r_2^2$ for every $t\in[0,1]$, that is, $|x(\gamma(t))|_{\mathrm e}\le r_2$. This proves (b) and completes the proof.

$$\ddot x^k+\Gamma^k{}_{ij}(x)\dot x^i\dot x^j=0\qquad(1\le k\le n),$$
with summation over repeated indices.

$$\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\sum_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k.$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

derivations.claim: (Speed bound.) Assume $v_0>0$. The geodesic velocity never vanishes: if it vanished at any parameter, uniqueness with that initial datum would make the geodesic constant, contradicting $v_0>0$ ([[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]). Thus $w>0$ on $[0,1]$, and let $t$ range over $[0,\delta]$, whose image is assumed to lie in $K$. By [L1], $w'\le\|\Gamma\|_K w^2$ and hence $(1/w)'=-w'/w^2\ge-\|\Gamma\|_K$ there; by [L2], $1/w(t)\ge 1/v_0-\|\Gamma\|_Kt$ and therefore $w(t)\le v_0/(1-\|\Gamma\|_Kv_0t)\le\frac43v_0$ for $4\|\Gamma\|_Kv_0t\le1$. If $v_0=0$, the constant curve has the same initial data as $\gamma$, so uniqueness of the geodesic initial-value problem gives $w\equiv0$. If $\|\Gamma\|_K=0$, the geodesic equation gives $\ddot x=0$ on the subinterval in $K$, so $w=v_0$ and the velocity change is zero. These cases use no reciprocal of $\|\Gamma\|_Kv_0$.

(Velocity-change bound.) On $[0,\delta]$ with $0\le\delta\le1$ and $4\|\Gamma\|_Kv_0\delta\le1$, steps 1.1 and [L3] give $\bigl|\dot x(t)-\dot x(0)\bigr|_{\mathrm e} \le\int_0^t\|\Gamma\|_K(4v_0/3)^2ds \le\|\Gamma\|_K v_0^2\,t\,\frac{16}9 \le\frac{4}{9}v_0$ for $4\|\Gamma\|_Kv_0t\le1$.

(Displacement along the initial direction.) Assume $v_0>0$, write $u_0:=\dot x(0)$ and $e:=u_0/v_0$, and put $\varphi(t):=e\cdot x(t)$. Then $\varphi'(0)=v_0$ and, by step 1.1, $\varphi''(t)=e\cdot\ddot x(t)\ge-\|\Gamma\|_K w(t)^2 \ge-\frac{16}9\|\Gamma\|_Kv_0^2$ for $t\le\delta$. Integrating twice on $[0,\delta]$ with $0\le\delta\le1$ and $4\|\Gamma\|_Kv_0\delta\le1$, $$\varphi(\delta)-\varphi(0)\ \ge\ v_0\delta-\frac{8}9\|\Gamma\|_Kv_0^2\delta^2\ =\ v_0\delta\Bigl(1-\frac89\|\Gamma\|_Kv_0\delta\Bigr)\ \ge\ \frac79\,v_0\delta .$$ If $v_0=0$ the displacement bound is trivial.

(Contained segments have small velocity.) Let $r>0$ satisfy $\|\Gamma\|_Kr\le\frac1{100}$ and $r\le\frac14$, let $\gamma:[0,1]\to U$ have image in $x^{-1}(B_r)$, and put $v_0=|\dot x(0)|_{\mathrm e}$. Suppose first that $\|\Gamma\|_Kv_0\le\frac14$. Then $\delta=1$ is admissible in steps 2.1-2.2, and also admissible trivially if $v_0=0$. Both $\gamma(0)$ and $\gamma(1)$ lie in $B_r$, so by [L4] $\bigl|x(\gamma(1))-x(\gamma(0))\bigr|_{\mathrm e}\le2r$; on the other hand the displacement's component along $u_0$ (the case $v_0=0$ is trivial) is at least $\frac79v_0$ by step 2.2, so $v_0\le\frac{18}7r<4r$. Suppose now that $\|\Gamma\|_Kv_0>\frac14$ and $v_0>0$; then $\delta=(4\|\Gamma\|_Kv_0)^{-1}<1$ is admissible, the points $\gamma(0)$ and $\gamma(\delta)$ both lie in $B_r$, so their displacement has norm at most $2r$, while step 2.2 gives a component along $u_0$ of at least $$\frac79\,v_0\delta=\frac7{36\|\Gamma\|_K}>2r,$$ the strict inequality because $\|\Gamma\|_Kr\le\frac1{100}<\frac7{72}$. This contradiction excludes the second case, so always $v_0<4r$. This proves (b).
Combining steps 1.1, 2.1, 2.2 and 3.1 proves (a) and (b) respectively.

boundaries.reason: The prescribed geodesic has a nonempty domain; a requirement that its restriction lie in empty K admits no such restriction.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 separates v_0=0 by geodesic uniqueness and Gamma norm zero by the coordinate equation. The time condition 4*norm(Gamma)*v_0*delta<=1 needs no reciprocal in these cases.

boundaries.reason: The single given geodesic is the object being bounded; no family cardinality is varied in clauses (a) or (b).

boundaries.evidence: Statement boundary: The constant geodesic is included when v_0=0. A zero Christoffel field has constant coordinate velocity and hence zero velocity change.
Statement boundary: The inequalities hold on the closed interval [0,delta]; delta=0 gives identical endpoints and zero displacement.

boundaries.reason: The positive-velocity direction e=u_0/v_0 in step 2.2 is fixed by the initial data; the zero branch is separate and selects no direction.
Contained-segment small-velocity is a sufficient conclusion under the radius assumptions, not a characterization of containment.
An initially small velocity is not asserted to guarantee that a whole geodesic stays in the coordinate ball.

For an affine connection as in [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]] and coordinates $(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, its **Christoffel symbols** in this chart are the unique smooth functions $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ such that
$$\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\sum_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k.$$
The first lower index $i$ is the differentiating direction and the second lower index $j$ labels the differentiated vector field. In the coordinate frame, the one-forms from [[def-connection-one-form-in-a-local-frame]] are $\omega^k{}_j=\sum_i\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\,dx^i$. A different chart generally has different symbols. This definition asserts neither symmetry in $i,j$ nor tensorial transformation.

For dimension one there is one smooth coefficient $\Gamma^1{}_{11}$; in dimension zero there are no coefficients. All statements are local, and at a boundary chart the derivatives are the smooth up-to-boundary coordinate derivatives.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), whose geodesics
and exponential map are those of [[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]].

**(a) Point-normal charts.** For every $p\in M$ there is a smooth chart
$(U,x)$ around $p$ with $x(p)=0$ such that, in the components of this chart,

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(p)=0,\qquad \partial_ag_{bc}(p)=0,\qquad g_{ab}(p)=\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}.$$

The construction starts from any chart around $p$ and is finite: no frame field
on $U$ and no global trivialization of $TM$ is used.

**(b) Exponential charts.** For every $p\in M$ and every $g_p$-orthonormal
basis $e_0,\dots,e_3$ of $T_pM$ there is a star-shaped open neighborhood
$W\subseteq T_pM$ of $0$ on which $\exp_p$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open
$U_p\ni p$, and the chart

$$u:=\psi\circ\exp_p^{-1}:U_p\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,$$

where $\psi:T_pM\to\mathbb R^4$ is the coordinate isomorphism of the basis,
satisfies $u(p)=0$ and the same three normal-form identities at $p$ as in (a).
Moreover every geodesic through $p$ has, in the chart $u$, the form
$u(\gamma(t))=(t-t_0)\,k$ for a constant $k\in\mathbb R^4$ whenever
$\gamma(t_0)=p$, $k=\psi(\gamma'(t_0))$, and
$(t-t_0)\gamma'(t_0)\in W$. Thus the portion represented by its radial initial
vector in $W$ is a straight coordinate ray through the origin. This claim is
not made for a later portion of a geodesic that may return to $U_p$ after its
radial initial vector has left $W$. No assertion is made about the second
derivatives of the metric at $p$: the construction is first order and does not
make a neighborhood of $p$ isometric to Minkowski space.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let
geodesics, their maximal domains $I_{q,v}$ and the exponential maps
$\exp_q$ be those of [[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]. Fix
$p\in M$. Write $\pi:TM\to M$ for the bundle projection.

**(a) Smoothness of the joint map.** The set
$$\mathcal D:=\{(q,v)\in TM:\ 1\in I_{q,v}\}\subseteq TM$$
is open in $TM$, and the **joint exponential map**
$$\Phi:\mathcal D\longrightarrow M\times M,\qquad \Phi(q,v):=(q,\exp_q v),$$
is smooth.

**(b) Differential at $(p,0)$.** The differential $d\Phi_{(p,0)}$ is an
isomorphism. Explicitly, fix a smooth chart $(U,x)$ around $p$; it induces
the chart $(TU,Tx)$ of $TM$ and the product chart $(U\times U,x\times x)$ of
$M\times M$, and under the induced identifications
$T_{(p,0)}(TM)\cong T_pM\oplus T_pM$ and
$T_{(p,p)}(M\times M)\cong T_pM\oplus T_pM$ one has
$$d\Phi_{(p,0)}(u,w)=(u,\ u+w)\qquad\text{for all }u,w\in T_pM .$$

**(c) Diffeomorphism and two-point inverse.** There are open neighborhoods
$V\subseteq\mathcal D$ of $(p,0)$ and $W\subseteq M\times M$ of $(p,p)$ such
that $\Phi|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Moreover $V$ can be chosen
product-like: there are a chart $(U,x)$ around $p$ with $x(p)=0$, a radius
$r>0$ and a velocity radius $\rho>0$ such that, writing $B_s:=\{y\in\mathbb
R^4:|y|_{\mathrm e}<s\}$,
$$V=\bigl\{(q,v):\ q\in x^{-1}(B_r),\ \text{the coordinate components of }v\text{ in }(TU,Tx)\text{ lie in }B_\rho\bigr\},$$
and there is $s\in(0,r)$ with $x^{-1}(\overline{B_s})\times x^{-1}(\overline{B_s})\subseteq W$.
Consequently the velocity map
$$v:W\longrightarrow TM,\qquad (q,r)\longmapsto v(q,r):=\text{the vector with }(q,v(q,r))\in V,\ \Phi(q,v(q,r))=(q,r),$$
is well defined and smooth, and $\exp_q\bigl(v(q,r)\bigr)=r$ for all
$(q,r)\in W$.

**(d) Lipschitz bound for the two-point inverse.** On every pair
$x^{-1}(B_s)\times x^{-1}(B_s)\subseteq W$ as in (c) there is a constant
$\Lambda\ge 0$ such that, for all $q,r\in x^{-1}(B_s)$,
$$|v(q,r)|_x\le\Lambda\,\bigl|x(q)-x(r)\bigr|_{\mathrm e},$$
where $|v|_x$ denotes the Euclidean norm of the coordinate components of
$v$ and $v(q,q)=0$. In particular $|v(q,r)|_x\le 2\Lambda s$ on this pair.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]) and let geodesics be those of
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]. Let $(U,x)$ be a smooth
chart of $M$ and write $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ with its Euclidean norm
$|\cdot|_{\mathrm e}$ on $x(U)\subseteq\mathbb R^4$; write
$B_s:=\{y\in\mathbb R^4:|y|_{\mathrm e}<s\}$ and, for a compact subset
$K\subseteq U$, let
$$\|\Gamma\|_K:=\sup_{y\in x(K)}\ \sup_{|u|_{\mathrm e}=|v|_{\mathrm e}=1}|\Gamma(y)[u,v]|_{\mathrm e},$$
where $\Gamma(y)[u,v]^a=\sum_{b,c=0}^3\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(y)u^bv^c$. Thus this is the Euclidean bilinear operator norm, not the maximum of the individual coefficients; set $\|\Gamma\|_{\varnothing}=0$. The Christoffel symbols are the smooth chart functions of
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]].

**(a) Second-derivative inequality.** Let $\gamma:J\to U$ be a geodesic and
let $f:J\to\mathbb R$, $f(t):=|x(\gamma(t))|_{\mathrm e}^2$, where the norm is
the Euclidean norm of the chart image. At every parameter $t\in J$,
$$f''(t)=2\bigl|\dot x(t)\bigr|_{\mathrm e}^2-2\,x(t)\cdot\Gamma(x(t))[\dot x(t),\dot x(t)],$$
where $\Gamma(x)[\dot x,\dot x]$ is the vector with components
$\sum_{i,j}\Gamma^a{}_{ij}(x)\dot x^i\dot x^j$ and $\cdot$ is the Euclidean
scalar product. Consequently, along every geodesic whose image lies in a
fixed compact $K\subseteq U$,
$$f''\ge 2\bigl(1-\|\Gamma\|_K\,|x(\gamma)|\bigr)\bigl|\dot x\bigr|_{\mathrm e}^2 .$$
In particular, if $x(K)\subseteq B_{r_1}$ and $\|\Gamma\|_K\,r_1\le\tfrac12$
then $f''\ge|\dot x|_{\mathrm e}^2\ge0$ at every parameter of such a
geodesic.

**(b) Maximum principle.** Let $\gamma:[0,1]\to U$ be a geodesic whose image
is contained in a compact $K$ with $x(K)\subseteq B_{r_1}$ and
$\|\Gamma\|_K\,r_1\le\frac12$, and suppose
$|x(\gamma(0))|_{\mathrm e}\le r_2$ and $|x(\gamma(1))|_{\mathrm e}\le r_2$
for some $r_2<r_1$. Then
$$|x(\gamma(t))|_{\mathrm e}\le r_2\qquad\text{for every }t\in[0,1].$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]) and geodesics as in
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]. Let $(U,x)$ be a chart,
$B_s=\{y\in\mathbb R^4:|y|_{\mathrm e}<s\}$ and let $K\subseteq U$ be compact
with $\|\Gamma\|_K<\infty$ as in
[[lem-gr-coordinate-ball-geodesic-convexity]]. Let $\gamma:[0,1]\to U$ be a
geodesic, write $s\mapsto w(s):=|\dot x(s)|_{\mathrm e}$ for the Euclidean
norm of its coordinate velocity, and let
$$v_0:=w(0).$$

**(a) Two-sided speed bounds.** If $0\le\delta\le1$, $4\|\Gamma\|_K v_0\delta\le1$, and the restriction of $\gamma$ to $[0,\delta]$ has image in $K$, then, for $t\in[0,\delta]$,
$$w(t)\le\frac43 v_0,\qquad\bigl|\dot x(t)-\dot x(0)\bigr|_{\mathrm e}\le\frac49 v_0 .$$
Consequently, when $v_0>0$, the Euclidean coordinate displacement has component at least $\frac59 v_0\delta$ along the unit vector $\dot x(0)/v_0$. When $v_0=0$, the geodesic is constant and the displacement is zero, so no unit initial direction is selected.

**(b) Contained segments have small velocity.** Let $c_0:=\frac1{100}$.
Fix $r>0$ with $r\le\frac14$ and $\|\Gamma\|_K\,r\le c_0$. If the image of
the geodesic $\gamma:[0,1]\to U$ is contained in $K\cap x^{-1}(B_r)$, then
$$|\dot x(0)|_{\mathrm e}\le 4r .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]) and let geodesics be those of
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]. Let $(U,x)$ be a smooth
chart of $M$ and write $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ with its Euclidean norm
$|\cdot|_{\mathrm e}$ on $x(U)\subseteq\mathbb R^4$; write
$B_s:=\{y\in\mathbb R^4:|y|_{\mathrm e}<s\}$ and, for a compact subset
$K\subseteq U$, let
$$\|\Gamma\|_K:=\sup_{y\in x(K)}\ \sup_{|u|_{\mathrm e}=|v|_{\mathrm e}=1}|\Gamma(y)[u,v]|_{\mathrm e},$$
where $\Gamma(y)[u,v]^a=\sum_{b,c=0}^3\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(y)u^bv^c$. Thus this is the Euclidean bilinear operator norm, not the maximum of the individual coefficients; set $\|\Gamma\|_{\varnothing}=0$. The Christoffel symbols are the smooth chart functions of
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]].

**(a) Second-derivative inequality.** Let $\gamma:J\to U$ be a geodesic and
let $f:J\to\mathbb R$, $f(t):=|x(\gamma(t))|_{\mathrm e}^2$, where the norm is
the Euclidean norm of the chart image. At every parameter $t\in J$,
$$f''(t)=2\bigl|\dot x(t)\bigr|_{\mathrm e}^2-2\,x(t)\cdot\Gamma(x(t))[\dot x(t),\dot x(t)],$$
where $\Gamma(x)[\dot x,\dot x]$ is the vector with components
$\sum_{i,j}\Gamma^a{}_{ij}(x)\dot x^i\dot x^j$ and $\cdot$ is the Euclidean
scalar product. Consequently, along every geodesic whose image lies in a
fixed compact $K\subseteq U$,
$$f''\ge 2\bigl(1-\|\Gamma\|_K\,|x(\gamma)|\bigr)\bigl|\dot x\bigr|_{\mathrm e}^2 .$$
In particular, if $x(K)\subseteq B_{r_1}$ and $\|\Gamma\|_K\,r_1\le\tfrac12$
then $f''\ge|\dot x|_{\mathrm e}^2\ge0$ at every parameter of such a
geodesic.

**(b) Maximum principle.** Let $\gamma:[0,1]\to U$ be a geodesic whose image
is contained in a compact $K$ with $x(K)\subseteq B_{r_1}$ and
$\|\Gamma\|_K\,r_1\le\frac12$, and suppose
$|x(\gamma(0))|_{\mathrm e}\le r_2$ and $|x(\gamma(1))|_{\mathrm e}\le r_2$
for some $r_2<r_1$. Then
$$|x(\gamma(t))|_{\mathrm e}\le r_2\qquad\text{for every }t\in[0,1].$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection, whose existence and uniqueness are
supplied by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; its
Christoffel symbols are the smooth chart functions of
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]. Recall that a **geodesic**
is a curve with $D_t\gamma'=0$ in its parameter
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]).

**(a) Local existence, uniqueness and maximality.** For every $(p,v)\in TM$
there is a unique maximal geodesic $\gamma_{p,v}:I_{p,v}\to M$ with
$\gamma_{p,v}(0)=p$ and $\gamma_{p,v}'(0)=v$; its domain $I_{p,v}$ is an open
interval containing $0$ and is not asserted to be all of $\mathbb R$.

**(b) Smooth dependence.** The set
$\mathcal G:=\{(t,p,v):t\in I_{p,v}\}\subseteq\mathbb R\times TM$ is open, and
the evaluation map $(t,p,v)\mapsto\gamma_{p,v}(t)$ is smooth on $\mathcal G$.

**(c) Scaling.** For every $s\in\mathbb R$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$,
$t\in I_{p,sv}$ if and only if $st\in I_{p,v}$, and then
$\gamma_{p,sv}(t)=\gamma_{p,v}(st)$.

**(d) The exponential map.** Define $\mathcal E_p:=\{v\in T_pM:1\in I_{p,v}\}$
and $\exp_p:\mathcal E_p\to M$, $\exp_p(v):=\gamma_{p,v}(1)$, and let
$\psi_p:T_pM\to\mathbb R^4$ be the coordinate isomorphism of a basis
$e_0,\dots,e_3$ of $T_pM$. Then $\mathcal E_p$ is open and star-shaped about
$0$ (if $v\in\mathcal E_p$ and $0\le s\le1$, then $sv\in\mathcal E_p$),
$\exp_p$ is smooth, $\exp_p(0)=p$, and, under the canonical identification
$T_0(T_pM)\cong T_pM$ induced by the chart $\psi_p$ on $T_pM$,
$$d(\exp_p)_0=\operatorname{id}_{T_pM}.$$
Consequently there is a star-shaped open neighborhood $W_p\subseteq\mathcal E_p$
of $0$ such that $\exp_p|_{W_p}$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of
$M$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let
geodesics, their maximal domains $I_{q,v}$ and the exponential maps
$\exp_q$ be those of [[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]. Fix
$p\in M$. Write $\pi:TM\to M$ for the bundle projection.

**(a) Smoothness of the joint map.** The set
$$\mathcal D:=\{(q,v)\in TM:\ 1\in I_{q,v}\}\subseteq TM$$
is open in $TM$, and the **joint exponential map**
$$\Phi:\mathcal D\longrightarrow M\times M,\qquad \Phi(q,v):=(q,\exp_q v),$$
is smooth.

**(b) Differential at $(p,0)$.** The differential $d\Phi_{(p,0)}$ is an
isomorphism. Explicitly, fix a smooth chart $(U,x)$ around $p$; it induces
the chart $(TU,Tx)$ of $TM$ and the product chart $(U\times U,x\times x)$ of
$M\times M$, and under the induced identifications
$T_{(p,0)}(TM)\cong T_pM\oplus T_pM$ and
$T_{(p,p)}(M\times M)\cong T_pM\oplus T_pM$ one has
$$d\Phi_{(p,0)}(u,w)=(u,\ u+w)\qquad\text{for all }u,w\in T_pM .$$

**(c) Diffeomorphism and two-point inverse.** There are open neighborhoods
$V\subseteq\mathcal D$ of $(p,0)$ and $W\subseteq M\times M$ of $(p,p)$ such
that $\Phi|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Moreover $V$ can be chosen
product-like: there are a chart $(U,x)$ around $p$ with $x(p)=0$, a radius
$r>0$ and a velocity radius $\rho>0$ such that, writing $B_s:=\{y\in\mathbb
R^4:|y|_{\mathrm e}<s\}$,
$$V=\bigl\{(q,v):\ q\in x^{-1}(B_r),\ \text{the coordinate components of }v\text{ in }(TU,Tx)\text{ lie in }B_\rho\bigr\},$$
and there is $s\in(0,r)$ with $x^{-1}(\overline{B_s})\times x^{-1}(\overline{B_s})\subseteq W$.
Consequently the velocity map
$$v:W\longrightarrow TM,\qquad (q,r)\longmapsto v(q,r):=\text{the vector with }(q,v(q,r))\in V,\ \Phi(q,v(q,r))=(q,r),$$
is well defined and smooth, and $\exp_q\bigl(v(q,r)\bigr)=r$ for all
$(q,r)\in W$.

**(d) Lipschitz bound for the two-point inverse.** On every pair
$x^{-1}(B_s)\times x^{-1}(B_s)\subseteq W$ as in (c) there is a constant
$\Lambda\ge 0$ such that, for all $q,r\in x^{-1}(B_s)$,
$$|v(q,r)|_x\le\Lambda\,\bigl|x(q)-x(r)\bigr|_{\mathrm e},$$
where $|v|_x$ denotes the Euclidean norm of the coordinate components of
$v$ and $v(q,q)=0$. In particular $|v(q,r)|_x\le 2\Lambda s$ on this pair.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map and let $p\in M$. If $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ is
an isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $U$ of $p$ and $V$ of
$F(p)$ such that $F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map and let $p\in M$. If $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ is
an isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $U$ of $p$ and $V$ of
$F(p)$ such that $F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism.

derivations.claim: (Setup and choice of $r$.) Fix the point-normal chart $(U,x)$ of [L1] and shrink it to satisfy [L2] with constants $r_0,\rho,\Lambda,s_0$. Since $\Gamma(p)=0$ by [L1] and the Christoffel symbols are continuous on the coordinate domain [L1], we may choose $r_1>0$ with $r_1\le r_0$ and $$\|\Gamma\|_{\overline{B_{r_1}}}\,r_1\le\tfrac1{100},\qquad r_1\le\tfrac14,\qquad x^{-1}(B_{r_1})\subseteq O .$$ Choose $r>0$ with $$r\le\min\Bigl\{\frac{r_1}{8\Lambda''},\ \frac{s_0}2,\ \frac{\rho}{32\Lambda'},\ \frac{1}{100\,\max(\Gamma_0\Lambda',1)},\ \frac14\Bigr\},$$ where $\Lambda':=\max(\Lambda,1)$, $\Lambda'':=\max(\tfrac83\Lambda,1)$ and $\Gamma_0:=\|\Gamma\|_{\overline{B_{r_1}}}$. Then $C=x^{-1}(B_r)\subseteq O\cap x^{-1}(B_{s_0})$.

(The two-point geodesic stays in the larger ball.) Let $q,q'\in\overline C$ and let $\Gamma_0:=\|\Gamma\|_{\overline{B_{r_1}}}$. Put $u:=v(q,q')\in T_qM$, so $|u|_x\le\Lambda|x(q)-x(q')|_{\mathrm e}\le 2\Lambda r\le \frac{\rho}{16}<\rho$ and $(q,u)\in V$; let $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$, $\gamma(t)=\exp_q(tu)$, be the corresponding geodesic. Since $|u|_x\le 2\Lambda r$ and $r\le\frac1{100\max(\Gamma_0\Lambda',1)}$, we have $4\Gamma_0|u|_x\le 8\Gamma_0\Lambda r\le\frac8{100}<1$, so $\delta=1$ satisfies $4\Gamma_0|u|_x\delta\le1$; [L3] then gives, as long as the image stays in $x^{-1}(B_{r_1})$, $$\bigl|\dot x(t)\bigr|_{\mathrm e}\le\tfrac43|u|_x\le\tfrac83\Lambda r,\qquad \bigl|x(\gamma(t))-x(q)\bigr|_{\mathrm e}\le\tfrac83\Lambda r .$$ Since $|x(q)|_{\mathrm e}\le r$ and $\frac83\Lambda r\le r_1/8<r_1-r$ by the choice of $r$, an exit from $x^{-1}(B_{r_1})$ at the first parameter $T$ would require displacement at least $r_1-r$, while the speed estimate bounds it by $\frac83\Lambda r$. This is a contradiction; hence the whole image lies in $x^{-1}(B_{r_1})$.

(Interior containment for distinct endpoints.) By step 2.1 the image of $\gamma$ lies in $x^{-1}(B_{r_1})$. Its endpoints satisfy $|x(q)|_{\mathrm e},|x(q')|_{\mathrm e}\le r$, and $\|\Gamma\|_{\overline{B_{r_1}}}r_1\le\frac1{100}\le\frac12$; [L4] applied with $r_2=r<r_1$ gives $|x(\gamma(t))|_{\mathrm e}\le r$ on $[0,1]$. If $q\ne q'$ and $|x(\gamma(t_0))|_{\mathrm e}=r$ for some $t_0\in(0,1)$, the convex function $f(t)=|x(\gamma(t))|_{\mathrm e}^2$ attains its maximum $r^2$ at an interior point, hence is constant by [L4]. Then $f''\equiv0$ while [L4] gives $f''\ge|\dot x|_{\mathrm e}^2$, so $\dot x\equiv0$ and $\gamma$ is constant, contradicting $q\ne q'$. Thus $\gamma((0,1))\subset C$ for distinct endpoints. If $q=q'$, then $v(q,q)=0$ by [L2] and $\gamma$ is the constant geodesic.

(Uniqueness on the closure.) Let $\eta:[0,1]\to\overline C$ be any geodesic segment from $q$ to $q'$. No interior-containment assumption is needed for this uniqueness argument. Its image lies in $\overline{B_r}\subset x^{-1}(\overline{B_{r_1}})$. For every $r'\in(r,r_1)$, apply [L3](b) with compact set $K=x^{-1}(\overline{B_{r_1}})$ and radius $r'$; its hypotheses hold because $r'<r_1\le1/4$ and $\Gamma_0r'\le\Gamma_0r_1\le1/100$. The image lies in $K\cap x^{-1}(B_{r'})$, so $|\dot x_\eta(0)|_{\mathrm e}\le4r'$. Letting $r'\downarrow r$ gives $|\dot x_\eta(0)|_{\mathrm e}\le4r\le\rho/(8\Lambda')<\rho$. Thus $(q,\eta'(0))\in V$ and $\Phi(q,\eta'(0))=(q,q')=\Phi(q,v(q,q'))$. Injectivity of $\Phi|_V$ gives $\eta'(0)=v(q,q')$, and uniqueness for the geodesic initial-value problem gives $\eta=\gamma$. This also excludes every nonconstant geodesic loop in $\overline C$ when $q=q'$, so the unique degenerate segment is constant. Together with step 3.1 this proves the closure-endpoint condition in the definition and the uniqueness assertion in (b).

(The domains $W_q$.) Fix $q\in C$ and let $W_q$ be as in (a). It is star-shaped by construction: if $u\in W_q$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$, the segment $t\mapsto\exp_q(t\lambda u)$, $t\in[0,1]$, is the initial arc of $t\mapsto\exp_q(tu)$ by the scaling rule of [[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]] clause (c), hence lies in $C$ and $\lambda u\in W_q$. It is open: if $u\in W_q$, the geodesic $\gamma_{q,u}$ is defined on $[0,1]$ with image in the open set $C$; choosing $\varepsilon>0$ with $\gamma_{q,u}([0,1+\varepsilon])\subset C$ (possible by [L5] since $\gamma_{q,u}(1)\in C$ is an interior point and the geodesic extends) and using smooth dependence on initial data [L5], all $u'$ sufficiently close to $u$ have $\gamma_{q,u'}([0,1+\varepsilon])\subset C$, so $u'\in W_q$. And $\exp_q(W_q)=C$: the inclusion $\subseteq$ is by definition of $W_q$; for $q'\in C$ the velocity $v(q,q')$ lies in $W_q$ by step 3.1 and $\exp_q(v(q,q'))=q'$.

($\exp_q:W_q\to C$ is a diffeomorphism.) It is smooth because $\exp_q$ is smooth on its domain [L5]; it is surjective by step 4.2; it is injective: if $\exp_q(u)=\exp_q(u')=q'$ with $u,u'\in W_q$, then the segments of $u$ and $u'$ lie in $C$, so [L3] gives $|u|_x,|u'|_x\le4r<\rho$; hence $(q,u),(q,u')\in V$ and $\Phi(q,u)=(q,q')=\Phi(q,u')$ forces $u=u'$. Finally, for $u\in W_q$ we have $|u|_x\le4r<\rho$ and $q\in x^{-1}(B_r)\subseteq x^{-1}(B_{s_0})$, so $(q,u)\in V$ and $d(\exp_q)_u$ is invertible by [L5]. A bijective local diffeomorphism onto $C$ is a diffeomorphism by [L6]. This proves (a).

(Conclusion.) Steps 2.1, 3.1 and 4.1 establish (b); steps 4.2 and 5.1 establish (a); together with the definitions of [[def-gr-normal-neighborhoods-and-position-vectors]] this gives (c). This completes the proof.

boundaries.reason: The given point p lies in O, and the constructed C contains p; an empty prescribed O cannot satisfy the hypothesis.

boundaries.evidence: Statement boundary: The proof takes positive upper bounds for inverse-velocity constants and max(Gamma norm,1) before radius reciprocals; constant joining curves are included when q=q-prime.
Statement boundary: For q=q-prime the unique contained geodesic is constant, with inverse velocity zero and the star-shaped domain still containing zero.

boundaries.reason: The local inverse differential is nonsingular; singular exponential charts are excluded by the inverse-function neighborhood.

boundaries.evidence: Statement boundary: Steps 2.1-4.2 control whole closed radial intervals [0,1]; open-ball containment is proved before claiming a joining segment stays in C.

boundaries.reason: The point-normal chart and finitely many positive radii are selected at the one prescribed p, without a global point-indexed choice function.
The unique-contained-geodesic and normal-domain properties are conclusions of a small-ball construction, not an iff characterization of balls.
No reverse implication says every set with one unique joining segment has all the stated normal-neighborhood properties.

risk_review.notes: Checked all seven construction steps: radii give a first-exit contradiction, strict convexity controls closure endpoints, contained-speed bounds force uniqueness in the joint inverse domain, W_q is open/star-shaped and the exponential is bijective with invertible derivative. Degenerate closure endpoints use the constant segment. The strengthened closed-product supplier supports the same construction.

citations.quote:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let $p\in M$.
Let $W_p\subseteq T_pM$ be a star-shaped open neighborhood of $0$ on which
$\exp_p$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open set $U_p:=\exp_p(W_p)$, as supplied
by [[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]] and
[[thm-gr-point-normal-and-exponential-coordinate-charts]]; identify
$T_v(T_pM)$ with $T_pM$ for every $v$.

**(a) Gauss lemma.** For every $v\in W_p$ and every $w\in T_pM$,

$$g_{\exp_pv}\bigl(d(\exp_p)_v(v),\,d(\exp_p)_v(w)\bigr)=g_p(v,w).$$

**(b) Radial maximum.** Let $\alpha:[0,1]\to U_p$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ future
timelike curve with $\alpha(0)=p$, with nonzero future timelike one-sided
tangents, set $q:=\alpha(1)$ and $v_q:=\exp_p^{-1}(q)$. Then

$$L_g(\alpha)\le\sqrt{-g_p(v_q,v_q)},$$

and equality holds if and only if there are $v_0\in W_p$ and a piecewise-$C^1$
strictly increasing surjection $\rho:[0,1]\to[0,\rho(1)]$ with
$v_q=\rho(1)v_0$ and $\alpha(t)=\exp_p(\rho(t)v_0)$ for all $t$; that is,
$\alpha$ is a monotone reparametrization of the radial geodesic segment from
$p$ to $q$. Dividing by $c$, the proper-time increment of $\alpha$ is at most
$\frac1c\sqrt{-g_p(v_q,v_q)}$, which is the proper-time increment of that
radial geodesic.

**(a) Local existence, uniqueness and maximality.** For every $(p,v)\in TM$
