citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]) for the absolutely continuous causal-curve
calculus and the supplied causal results used below.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]). Let $C\subseteq M$ be a strictly
convex normal set ([[def-gr-normal-neighborhoods-and-position-vectors]]
clause (b)), let $p\in C$, and write
$$W_p:=\exp_p^{-1}(C)\subseteq T_pM,\qquad v(q):=\exp_p^{-1}(q),\qquad P(p,q):=d(\exp_p)_{v(q)}(v(q)),\qquad D_p^2(q):=g_p(v(q),v(q)).$$
Define
$$J_C^+(p):=\{p\}\cup\{q\in C:\text{there is a future causal curve } \sigma:[0,1]\to C\text{ with }\sigma(0)=p,\ \sigma(1)=q\},$$
so the reflexive endpoint $p$ is included even though a constant curve is
not in the curve class. Define
$$I_C^+(p):=\{q\in C:\text{there is a future timelike curve } \sigma:[0,1]\to C\text{ with }\sigma(0)=p,\ \sigma(1)=q\}$$
([[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]). Put
$$\mathcal C^+:=\{v\in W_p:v\text{ is future causal or }v=0\},\quad \mathcal T^+:=\{v\in W_p:v\text{ is future timelike}\},\quad \mathcal N^+:=\{v\in W_p:v\text{ is future null and }v\ne0\}.$$
Then:

**(a) Causal containment.** For every future causal curve
$\sigma:[0,1]\to C$ with $\sigma(0)=p$, the position vector
$v(\sigma(t))$ is future causal or zero for every $t\in[0,1]$.

**(b) Cone characterizations.**
$$J^+_C(p)=\exp_p(\mathcal C^+),\qquad I^+_C(p)=\exp_p(\mathcal T^+),\qquad J^+_C(p)\setminus\bigl(I^+_C(p)\cup\{p\}\bigr)=\exp_p(\mathcal N^+).$$

**(c) Null rigidity.** Let $\sigma:[0,1]\to C$ be future causal with
$\sigma(0)=p$, and let $\hat s\in(0,1]$ satisfy: $v(\sigma(\hat s))$ is
future null nonzero and $v(\sigma(t))\ne0$ for every $t\in(0,\hat s]$. Then
there are $v_0\in\mathcal N^+$ and a nondecreasing absolutely continuous
surjection $\varphi:[0,\hat s]\to[0,1]$ with
$\sigma(t)=\exp_p(\varphi(t)v_0)$ for $0\le t\le\hat s$.

**(d) Length maximality.** Let $\sigma:[0,1]\to C$ be future causal with
$\sigma(0)=p$. Then
$$L_g(\sigma)\le\sqrt{-D_p^2\bigl(\sigma(1)\bigr)}=\sqrt{-g_p\bigl(v(\sigma(1)),v(\sigma(1))\bigr)} .$$
If moreover $v(\sigma(1))$ is future timelike and $v(\sigma(t))\ne0$ for all
$t\in(0,1]$, then equality holds if and only if there are $v_0$ future
timelike and a nondecreasing absolutely continuous surjection
$\varphi:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ with $\sigma(t)=\exp_p(\varphi(t)v_0)$ for all $t$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), and let $\exp_q:\mathcal E_q\to M$
be the exponential maps of
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]. For an open set
$U\subseteq M$ write $T U\subseteq TM$ for the tangent vectors based at
points of $U$.

**(a) Normal neighborhood.** An open neighborhood $U$ of $p\in M$ is a
**normal neighborhood of $p$** when there is an open star-shaped subset
$W\subseteq\mathcal E_p$ of $T_pM$ such that $U=\exp_p(W)$ and
$\exp_p|_W:W\to U$ is a diffeomorphism onto $U$
([[thm-gr-point-normal-and-exponential-coordinate-charts]] clause (b)
supplies such pairs). The **exponential coordinates at $p$** on such a $U$
are $u:=\psi\circ\exp_p^{-1}:U\to\mathbb R^4$ for a linear isomorphism
$\psi:T_pM\to\mathbb R^4$.

**(b) Convex normal and strictly convex normal sets.** An open set
$C\subseteq M$ is **convex normal** when it is a normal neighborhood of each
of its points; thus for every $q\in C$ there is an open star-shaped
$C_q\subseteq\mathcal E_q$ with $\exp_q(C_q)=C$ and
$\exp_q|_{C_q}$ a diffeomorphism onto $C$. It is **strictly convex normal**
when it is convex normal and every pair $q,q'\in\overline C$ is joined by exactly one affinely
parametrized geodesic segment $\gamma:[0,1]\to\overline C$ with
$\gamma(0)=q$ and $\gamma(1)=q'$, and, if $q\ne q'$, its parameter interior
$\gamma((0,1))$ lies in $C$. In the degenerate case $q=q'$, the required
segment is the constant geodesic at $q$; no interior-containment condition
is imposed on this degenerate segment when $q\in\partial C$.

**(c) Position vector.** Fix a normal neighborhood $U=\exp_p(W)$ of $p$
as in (a), with its chosen inverse $(\exp_p|_W)^{-1}$, and let $q\in U$.
Put $v:=(\exp_p|_W)^{-1}(q)\in T_pM$. Since $W$ is star-shaped,
$tv\in W$ for $0\le t\le1$, and
$x(t):=\exp_p(tv)$ is the radial geodesic segment in $U$ from $p$ to $q$.
The vector
$$P(p,q):=\gamma_{p,v}'(1)=d(\exp_p)_{v}(v)\in T_qM$$
is the **position vector of $q$ with respect to $p$**; here
$\gamma_{p,v}$ is the maximal geodesic of
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]. The notation $P(p,q)$
uses this chosen inverse branch; another normal neighborhood may select a
different radial segment for the same endpoints. On a convex normal set
$C$, use the inverse domains $C_p$ of (b) and the joining segment in $C$;
on a strictly convex normal set this segment is unique by (b).
By the Gauss lemma of
[[thm-gr-lorentz-gauss-lemma-and-normal-maximum]]
$g_q(P(p,q),P(p,q))=g_p(\exp_p^{-1}(q),\exp_p^{-1}(q))$.

**(d) Squared-displacement function.** For a normal neighborhood $U$ of
$p$ the **squared-displacement function** is
$$D_p^2:U\to\mathbb R,\qquad D_p^2(q):=g_p\bigl(\exp_p^{-1}(q),\exp_p^{-1}(q)\bigr).$$
It is smooth on $U$ because $\exp_p^{-1}$ is smooth and $g_p$ is bilinear;
$D_p^2(p)=0$, $D_p^2(q)<0$ exactly when $P(p,q)$ is timelike,
$D_p^2(q)=0$ exactly when $P(p,q)$ is null or zero, and $D_p^2(q)>0$
exactly when $P(p,q)$ is spacelike. On a convex normal $C$ we write
$D^2:C\times C\to\mathbb R$, $D^2(p,q):=D_p^2(q)$, whenever the position
vector is defined using these inverse domains.

**(e) Scope.** These are definitions inside the smooth Lorentzian model;
they assert no existence of convex normal sets (supplied separately by
[[thm-gr-convex-normal-neighborhoods]]), no completeness and no physical
reading. The position vector is an element of $T_qM$, not a vector field and
not a coordinate displacement; $D^2$ is not a metric distance and takes
negative values on timelike-separated pairs.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), let $p\in M$ and let $U_p=\exp_p(W_p)$
be a normal neighborhood of $p$ with $W_p$ star-shaped, as in
[[def-gr-normal-neighborhoods-and-position-vectors]] clause (a). Write
$v(q):=\exp_p^{-1}(q)$ for $q\in U_p$, $P(p,q):=d(\exp_p)_{v(q)}(v(q))$, and
$D_p^2(q):=g_p(v(q),v(q))$.

**(a) Differential in the second argument.** $D_p^2$ is smooth on $U_p$ and,
for every $q\in U_p$ and every $w\in T_qM$,
$$d(D_p^2)_q(w)=2\,g_q\bigl(P(p,q),w\bigr).$$

**(b) Reversal.** Let $q\in U_p$ and let $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$,
$\gamma(t)=\exp_p(t\,v(q))$, be the radial geodesic, so that
$\gamma(1)=q$. Then the reversed segment $t\mapsto\gamma(1-t)$ is the
restriction to $[0,1]$ of the maximal geodesic from $q$ with initial velocity
$-P(p,q)$; consequently
$$\exp_q^{-1}(p)=-P(p,q)\quad\text{and}\quad P(q,p)=-\,v(q)=-(\exp_p)^{-1}(q)$$
whenever the chosen normal inverse at $q$ has a domain containing
$-P(p,q)$. This condition holds in particular when both inverses are
those of one strictly convex normal set $C$ containing $p,q$ and the
inverse at $p$ used to define $v(q)$ is the one mapping $C$ to its
radial domain. Merely having $p,q\in C$ does not identify an independently
chosen inverse on $U_p$ with the inverse selected by $C$.
Under the inverse-domain condition, $D_q^2(p)=D_p^2(q)$ by the Gauss
lemma of [[thm-gr-lorentz-gauss-lemma-and-normal-maximum]].

**(c) Differential on pairs in a strictly convex normal set.** Use the inverse
domains selected by $C$ in this clause. If $C$ is a
strictly convex normal set ([[thm-gr-convex-normal-neighborhoods]]) and
$p,q\in C$, then
$D^2:C\times C\to\mathbb R$ is smooth and for all $u\in T_pM$, $w\in T_qM$,
$$dD^2(p,q)(u,w)=2\,g_p\bigl(P(q,p),u\bigr)+2\,g_q\bigl(P(p,q),w\bigr).$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let
geodesics, their maximal domains $I_{q,v}$ and the exponential maps
$\exp_q$ be those of [[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]. Fix
$p\in M$. Write $\pi:TM\to M$ for the bundle projection.

**(a) Smoothness of the joint map.** The set
$$\mathcal D:=\{(q,v)\in TM:\ 1\in I_{q,v}\}\subseteq TM$$
is open in $TM$, and the **joint exponential map**
$$\Phi:\mathcal D\longrightarrow M\times M,\qquad \Phi(q,v):=(q,\exp_q v),$$
is smooth.

**(b) Differential at $(p,0)$.** The differential $d\Phi_{(p,0)}$ is an
isomorphism. Explicitly, fix a smooth chart $(U,x)$ around $p$; it induces
the chart $(TU,Tx)$ of $TM$ and the product chart $(U\times U,x\times x)$ of
$M\times M$, and under the induced identifications
$T_{(p,0)}(TM)\cong T_pM\oplus T_pM$ and
$T_{(p,p)}(M\times M)\cong T_pM\oplus T_pM$ one has
$$d\Phi_{(p,0)}(u,w)=(u,\ u+w)\qquad\text{for all }u,w\in T_pM .$$

**(c) Diffeomorphism and two-point inverse.** There are open neighborhoods
$V\subseteq\mathcal D$ of $(p,0)$ and $W\subseteq M\times M$ of $(p,p)$ such
that $\Phi|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Moreover $V$ can be chosen
product-like: there are a chart $(U,x)$ around $p$ with $x(p)=0$, a radius
$r>0$ and a velocity radius $\rho>0$ such that, writing $B_s:=\{y\in\mathbb
R^4:|y|_{\mathrm e}<s\}$,
$$V=\bigl\{(q,v):\ q\in x^{-1}(B_r),\ \text{the coordinate components of }v\text{ in }(TU,Tx)\text{ lie in }B_\rho\bigr\},$$
and there is $s\in(0,r)$ with $x^{-1}(\overline{B_s})\times x^{-1}(\overline{B_s})\subseteq W$.
Consequently the velocity map
$$v:W\longrightarrow TM,\qquad (q,r)\longmapsto v(q,r):=\text{the vector with }(q,v(q,r))\in V,\ \Phi(q,v(q,r))=(q,r),$$
is well defined and smooth, and $\exp_q\bigl(v(q,r)\bigr)=r$ for all
$(q,r)\in W$.

**(d) Lipschitz bound for the two-point inverse.** On every pair
$x^{-1}(B_s)\times x^{-1}(B_s)\subseteq W$ as in (c) there is a constant
$\Lambda\ge 0$ such that, for all $q,r\in x^{-1}(B_s)$,
$$|v(q,r)|_x\le\Lambda\,\bigl|x(q)-x(r)\bigr|_{\mathrm e},$$
where $|v|_x$ denotes the Euclidean norm of the coordinate components of
$v$ and $v(q,q)=0$. In particular $|v(q,r)|_x\le 2\Lambda s$ on this pair.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]) and geodesics as in
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]. Let $p\in M$ and let
$O\subseteq M$ be an open neighborhood of $p$. Then there are a chart
$(U,x)$ around $p$ with $x(p)=0$ and a radius $r>0$ such that
$C:=x^{-1}(B_r)$, $B_r=\{y\in\mathbb R^4:|y|_{\mathrm e}<r\}$ based at
$0=x(p)$, is contained in $O$ and has the following properties.

**(a) Normal neighborhood of each point.** For every $q\in C$ define
$$W_q:=\bigl\{u\in\mathcal E_q:\ \exp_q(tu)\in C\ \text{for every }t\in[0,1]\bigr\},$$
where $\mathcal E_q$ is the exponential domain of
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]] clause (d). Then $W_q$ is an
open star-shaped neighborhood of $0$ in $T_qM$, and
$\exp_q|_{W_q}:W_q\to C$ is a diffeomorphism onto $C$.

**(b) Unique contained joining segment.** For all $q,q'\in C$ there is
exactly one geodesic segment joining $q$ to $q'$ whose image is contained in
$C$, namely
$$x_{q,q'}:[0,1]\to C,\qquad x_{q,q'}(t)=\exp_q\bigl(t\,v(q,q')\bigr),$$
where $v(q,q')$ is the two-point inverse velocity of
[[lem-gr-joint-exponential-diffeomorphism]] clause (c). For $q\ne q'$ the
points $x_{q,q'}(t)$, $0<t<1$, lie in $C$ strictly inside the coordinate
ball, i.e. $|x(x_{q,q'}(t))|_{\mathrm e}<r$; and $x_{q',q}$ is the time
reverse of $x_{q,q'}$ up to affine reparametrization.

**(c) Strict convexity.** In the terminology of
[[def-gr-normal-neighborhoods-and-position-vectors]] clause (b), $C$ is a
strictly convex normal neighborhood; in particular the position vector
$P(q,q')=d(\exp_q)_{v(q,q')}\bigl(v(q,q')\bigr)$ and the squared
displacement $D^2(q,q')=g_q\bigl(v(q,q'),v(q,q')\bigr)$ are defined for all
$q,q'\in C$.

For the absolutely continuous curve conclusion (c), assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]) as required by the cited causal-curve calculus and fundamental theorem. The other clauses use the given smooth observer structure, pointwise adapted-chart existence and finite compactness arguments, without these additional curve-calculus premises. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), and put $n=N/\sqrt{-g(N,N)}$. Write $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. In a chart $(U,x)$ put $v^a=dx^a(v)$, $v_s=(v^1,v^2,v^3)$ and $|v|_{\mathrm e}=(\sum_{a=0}^3(v^a)^2)^{1/2}$.

**(a) Adapted orthonormal charts.** For every $p\in M$ there are a chart $(U,x)$, $x(p)=0$, a radius $r>0$ with $U=x^{-1}(B_r)$, and $K\ge1$, such that on all of $U$
$$n=\partial_{x^0},\qquad g_{00}\equiv-1,\qquad g_{ab}(p)=\eta_{ab}.$$

**(b) Cone domination.** The chart and radius in (a) can be chosen so every nonzero future causal vector at any point of $U$ satisfies
$$|v_s|\le K v^0,\qquad |v^i|\le K v^0\quad(i=1,2,3),\qquad v^0\ge K^{-1}|v|_{\mathrm e}>0.$$

**(c) Curve form.** Every future causal curve $\gamma:I\to U$ of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] has strictly increasing time coordinate, and for all $s<t$ in $I$
$$x^0(\gamma(s))<x^0(\gamma(t)),\qquad |x_s(\gamma(t))-x_s(\gamma(s))|\le K\left(x^0(\gamma(t))-x^0(\gamma(s))\right).$$
Consequently every spatial component satisfies the same bound, and the curve image is the graph of a $K$-Lipschitz function into Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$ over the interval $x^0(\gamma(I))$.

**(d) Flat minorant cone.** The same chart can be chosen so the constant-coordinate metric $\eta_{16}=-(dx^0)^2+16\sum_i(dx^i)^2$ has every nonzero $\eta_{16}$-causal vector $g$-timelike throughout $U$. If $q,q'\in U$ and $\eta_{16}(x(q')-x(q),x(q')-x(q))<0$, then $q\ll q'$ if $x^0(q')>x^0(q)$, and $q'\ll q$ otherwise.

**(e) General temporal charts: exact compact uniformity.** For any chart $(U',z)$ define its temporal locus
$$P=\{q\in U':\nabla z^0(q)\text{ is past timelike}\}.$$
For every compact set $K_0\subset P$ there is $L\ge1$ such that all nonzero future causal vectors based in $K_0$, with coordinate components and Euclidean norm taken in $z$, satisfy
$$|v_s|\le L v^0,\qquad |v^i|\le L v^0,\qquad v^0\ge L^{-1}|v|_{\mathrm e}>0.$$
In particular these bounds hold throughout any relatively compact $U_0\Subset U'$ whose closure is contained in $P$, equivalently whose time gradient is past timelike on its entire closure. Timelikeness merely on $U_0$ gives local bounds at each point and uniform bounds on each compact subset of $U_0$; it does not alone give a uniform bound on all of $U_0$.

No additional choice is used to select the pointwise linear bases or compact cone constants. Countable and Dependent Choice are explicitly required only for the general absolutely continuous curve clause (c), through its actual calculus suppliers.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $a\le b$ and $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]). The function $f$ is
**absolutely continuous** on $[a,b]$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$\delta>0$ such that every finite family of subintervals
$[u_j,v_j]\subseteq[a,b]$, indexed by $j<m$, whose open interiors are pairwise
disjoint and which satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}(v_j-u_j)<\delta$$

also satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}|f(v_j)-f(u_j)|<\varepsilon.$$

Finite sums and the empty sum are those of [[def-finite-sum]] and
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. For $m=0$ both sums are $0$, so the condition is
automatic. On $[a,a]$ every permitted interval is a singleton and every endpoint
increment is $0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), so every function on that singleton is
absolutely continuous. Absolute continuity implies ordinary continuity
([[def-continuity-real]]); that implication is proved next rather than built into
the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $F\in AC[a,b]$, then $F'$ exists almost everywhere on $(a,b)$ and belongs to
$L^1[a,b]$.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then
$$\lim_{r\to0^+}A_rf(x)=f(x)$$
for Lebesgue-almost every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of subsets of $\mathbb{R}$, each of
measure zero ([[def-measure-zero-and-content-zero]]). Then

$$\bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} A_n \quad \text{has measure zero.}$$

By the padding convention of [[def-measure-zero-and-content-zero]] and
[[def-countable]] the same conclusion covers the union of an at most countable
family of null sets, a finite family being extended by copies of $\varnothing$.

**The hypothesis $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is spent at exactly one step, step 2.1
below**, where one covering sequence is selected for every $A_n$ at once. Each
$A_n$ has many such covers and nullity provides no rule for singling one out.
Nothing else in the proof selects anything: the diagonal enumeration and the
estimate are formulas.

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   ([[def-countable]]).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

Let $(f_n)$ be nonnegative measurable functions. Then
$$\int \liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu.$$

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.
The topology of $d_g$ is the manifold topology on every connected Riemannian manifold.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the causal-curve class of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]].

**(a) Chart independence.** Local absolute continuity in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (a) is independent of the
chosen chart and of the smooth atlas. Every compact parameter interval
admits a finite subdivision on each of whose pieces a chart representative
is absolutely continuous. For a continuous curve, the relative neighborhood
formulation and the compact chart-interval formulation of that definition
are equivalent.

**(b) Velocity and smooth composition.** At every interior parameter value
$t$ at which one chart representative is differentiable, every chart
representative is differentiable, the velocity $\gamma'(t)$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (b) is well defined and
independent of the chart, and the set of parameter values at which some
chart representative is differentiable has full measure in the domain. For
every smooth map $F$ of an open subset of $M$ into a finite-dimensional
smooth manifold $P$ (in particular $P=\mathbb R$) whose domain contains
the image of $\gamma$, the composite $F\circ\gamma$ is locally absolutely
continuous in charts of $P$ using the same relative neighborhood definition,
and $(F\circ\gamma)'(t)=dF_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t))$ at almost
every parameter value $t$.

**(c) Piecewise $C^1$ curves.** Every piecewise $C^1$ curve (with the finite
admissible partition and one-sided endpoint convention of clause (a) of
[[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]) is locally absolutely
continuous; a piecewise $C^1$ curve all of whose tangents are future causal
is a future causal curve, and if in addition its tangents are future
timelike, it is a future timelike curve.

**(d) Concatenation.** If $\gamma_1:[a,b]\to M$ and $\gamma_2:[b,c]\to M$ are
future causal curves (respectively future timelike curves) with
$\gamma_1(b)=\gamma_2(b)$, then the concatenation $\gamma:[a,c]\to M$,
$\gamma(t):=\gamma_1(t)$ for $t\le b$ and $\gamma(t):=\gamma_2(t)$ for
$t\ge b$, is a future causal (respectively future timelike) curve; the same
holds for any finite chain of such curves.

**(e) Reparametrization.** If $\varphi:J\to I$ is a strictly increasing
$C^1$ diffeomorphism of intervals with $\varphi'>0$ and $\gamma:I\to M$ is
locally absolutely continuous, then $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is locally
absolutely continuous and $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is future causal (respectively
future timelike) exactly when $\gamma$ is. Moreover $\gamma$ is
future-inextendible if and only if $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is
future-inextendible, and this equivalence holds for every strictly increasing
continuous surjection $\varphi$ of intervals, not only the $C^1$ ones.

**(f) Relations.** The relation $\le$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] is reflexive and transitive, and
$p\ll q$ implies $p\le q$ for all $p,q$; the relations $J^{\pm}$ and
$I^{\pm}$ of that definition are therefore nested, $I^{\pm}(S)\subseteq
J^{\pm}(S)$ for every $S\subseteq M$.

derivations.claim: (Fixed local branches over the compact image.) Choose finitely many adapted charts $(V_j,x_j)$ and open sets $A_j$ covering the image of $\alpha$, with compact closures $K_j\subset V_j$. Shrink these sets using the joint exponential inverse of [L2], so that for each $j$ there is $\rho_j>0$ with the following properties. The joint exponential is defined and injective on all $(p,v)$ with $p\in K_j$ and $|v|_{x_j}\le\rho_j$; its smooth inverse branch $v_j(p,q)$ is defined near $K_j\times K_j$ and $|v_j(p,q)|_{x_j}<\rho_j/2$ there. Its radial geodesics stay in $V_j$ for $0\le\lambda\le1$. These choices follow by taking a closed product inside the open inverse-function domain near each diagonal point, then shrinking the coordinate ball: $v_j(p,p)=0$, and the geodesic with zero velocity is constant. Smoothness on these closed products gives uniform finite bounds, with one constant $C$ enlarged over the finite family, such that $|v_j(p,q)|_{x_j}\le C|x_j(q)-x_j(p)|,$ $v_j(p,q)=x_j(q)-x_j(p)+R_j(p,q),\qquad |R_j(p,q)|\le C|x_j(q)-x_j(p)|^2,$ where the tangent vector is expressed in the coordinate basis at $p$. The second estimate follows by integrating the second-variable derivative along the coordinate segment twice: its value at $q=p$ is the identity and its derivative is bounded on the compact product. Likewise, bounded first derivatives of the geodesic evaluation give $|x_j(\exp_p(\lambda v_j(p,q)))-x_j(p)|\le C|v_j(p,q)|\quad(0\le\lambda\le1).$ A Lebesgue number for the finite parameter cover $\alpha^{-1}(A_j)$ ensures that every sufficiently short parameter subarc lies in some $A_j$.

(The selected inverse cannot leave this branch.) Let a short subarc $\alpha([u,v])$ lie in $A_j$, and suppose also that it lies in any strictly convex normal ball $U$, with $p=\alpha(u)$. The selected lift $z(t):=\exp_{p,U}^{-1}(\alpha(t)),\qquad u\le t\le v,$ is continuous by [L2], with $z(u)=0$. Here the subscript $U$ specifies the inverse selected by that normal ball, not a different exponential map. If $|z(t)|_{x_j}$ ever reached $\rho_j$, let $t_*$ be its first such parameter. At $t_*$ both $z(t_*)$ and $v_j(p,\alpha(t_*))$ are in the fixed injectivity domain of step 1.1 and have the same exponential image. They must agree, contradicting the strict bound $|v_j|<\rho_j/2$. Consequently $|z(t)|<\rho_j$ throughout, and the same injectivity gives $\exp_{p,U}^{-1}(\alpha(t))=v_j(p,\alpha(t))\quad(u\le t\le v).$ Thus the inverse and joining geodesic selected by **each** $U_i^N$ agree with the fixed branch for all sufficiently fine partitions. No bound on the sizes, chart constants or injectivity radii of the varying $U_i^N$ is used.

(One integrable control.) Fix a finite subdivision $a=r_0<\cdots<r_m=b$ with each block image in one $A_j$ and define $w(t)$ on that block to be the Euclidean norm of $(x_j\circ\alpha)'(t)$, setting it to zero at the finitely many subdivision points. Local absolute continuity gives $w\ge0$, $w\in L^1[a,b]$. There is a uniform constant $C$ such that, in any selected chart containing a point of a block, $|(x_k\circ\alpha)'|\le Cw$ almost everywhere on the overlap. Indeed the transition derivatives are bounded on the intersections of the finitely many compact sets $K_j,K_k$; apply the chain rule. Thus, even when a fine partition interval $I_i=[t_i,t_{i+1}]$ crosses a fixed block boundary, finite integral additivity gives $|x_k(\alpha(t_{i+1}))-x_k(\alpha(t_i))| \le C\int_{I_i}w$ for the chart assigned to that entire short subarc. The metric components are bounded on the same compact sets, so the original Lorentzian density $f(t)=\sqrt{-g(\alpha'(t),\alpha'(t))}$ satisfies $f\le Cw$.

(Interpolants and uniform control.) For any of the promised partitions, write $h_i=t_{i+1}-t_i$, $p_i=\alpha(t_i)$ and let $v_i$ be the inverse selected by $U_i^N$. Concatenate its radial geodesics, affinely parametrized on $I_i$, to obtain $\gamma_N$. The endpoints are distinct because the adapted time of [L3] strictly increases along the original subarc. The cone theorem [L1] therefore makes each radial segment future causal; its length is $d_{U_i^N}(p_i,p_{i+1})$ and its constant Lorentzian speed is $f_N(t)=\frac{\sqrt{-g_{p_i}(v_i,v_i)}}{h_i}\quad(t\in\operatorname{int}I_i).$ By steps 1.1-2.1 and 2.2, for all sufficiently large $N$, $0\le f_N(t)\le Cw_N(t),\qquad w_N(t):=\frac1{h_i}\int_{I_i}w,\qquad \int_a^bw_N=\int_a^bw.$ The same estimates put the geodesic and the original subarc in the fixed chart, with their coordinate discrepancy bounded by $C\int_{I_i}w$. Absolute continuity of the integral of $w$ makes this bound tend to zero uniformly as the mesh tends to zero. Finite chart comparison therefore also proves $\gamma_N\to\alpha$ uniformly. Crucially all constants belong to the fixed finite charts, not the independently varying normal balls.

(Almost-everywhere speed convergence.) Outside a null set, $t$ is a Lebesgue point of $w$ and of every local coordinate derivative of $\alpha$ where its chart is defined (use countable compact exhaustions of each open parameter preimage of $V_j$), and is neither a fixed subdivision point nor any partition point. The latter points form a countable union of finite sets. For the interval $I_i$ containing such $t$, [L4] gives $w_N(t)\to w(t)$ and the coordinate secant velocity tends to the coordinate velocity of $\alpha$ at $t$. Step 1.1 has the precise error bound $\left|\frac{v_i}{h_i}-\frac{x_j(p_{i+1})-x_j(p_i)}{h_i}\right| \le C h_i w_N(t)^2\longrightarrow0.$ Here $w_N(t)$ is bounded at this Lebesgue point; there is no assertion of a uniform $o(h_i)$ error for an arbitrary absolutely continuous curve. Since only finitely many charts are possible, these pointwise conclusions hold even if their assigned index varies with $N$. Continuity of $g$, with $p_i\to\alpha(t)$, gives $f_N(t)\to f(t)$ almost everywhere.

(Fatou proves the full refined-sum identity.) Choose the common $C$ of step 3.1 also large enough that $f\le Cw$. The nonnegative functions $Cw_N-f_N$ converge almost everywhere to $Cw-f$. Fatou gives $C\int_a^bw-L_g(\alpha) \le\liminf_N\left(C\int_a^bw-\int_a^bf_N\right),$ hence $\limsup_N\int f_N\le L_g(\alpha)$. Conversely, [L1] on every original subarc gives $L_g(\alpha)\le\sum_i d_{U_i^N}(p_i,p_{i+1})=\int_a^bf_N.$ The two inequalities prove (a), including its independently varying-ball quantifier and independence of both the partitions and the chosen balls.

(Upper semicontinuity.) Choose a fixed finite buffered normal-ball cover of $\alpha([a,b])$ and successively finer partitions such that each compact subarc is contained in one cover ball. For any fixed such partition, uniform convergence puts the corresponding subarcs of $\alpha_k$ in those same open balls for every sufficiently large $k$. By [L1] and continuity of the finitely many selected inverse functions [L2], $\limsup_kL_g(\alpha_k) \le\sum_i d_{U_i}(\alpha(t_i),\alpha(t_{i+1})).$ Now refine the fixed-cover partitions and use (a), already proved without using (b), to make the right side tend to $L_g(\alpha)$. This proves (b).
The arbitrary-ball identity is step 5.1 and upper semicontinuity is step 6.1, proving both promised claims.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]) for the absolutely continuous causal-curve
calculus and the supplied causal results used below.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]). Let $C\subseteq M$ be a strictly
convex normal set ([[def-gr-normal-neighborhoods-and-position-vectors]]
clause (b)), let $p\in C$, and write
$$W_p:=\exp_p^{-1}(C)\subseteq T_pM,\qquad v(q):=\exp_p^{-1}(q),\qquad P(p,q):=d(\exp_p)_{v(q)}(v(q)),\qquad D_p^2(q):=g_p(v(q),v(q)).$$
Define
$$J_C^+(p):=\{p\}\cup\{q\in C:\text{there is a future causal curve } \sigma:[0,1]\to C\text{ with }\sigma(0)=p,\ \sigma(1)=q\},$$
so the reflexive endpoint $p$ is included even though a constant curve is
not in the curve class. Define
$$I_C^+(p):=\{q\in C:\text{there is a future timelike curve } \sigma:[0,1]\to C\text{ with }\sigma(0)=p,\ \sigma(1)=q\}$$
([[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]). Put
$$\mathcal C^+:=\{v\in W_p:v\text{ is future causal or }v=0\},\quad \mathcal T^+:=\{v\in W_p:v\text{ is future timelike}\},\quad \mathcal N^+:=\{v\in W_p:v\text{ is future null and }v\ne0\}.$$
Then:

**(a) Causal containment.** For every future causal curve
$\sigma:[0,1]\to C$ with $\sigma(0)=p$, the position vector
$v(\sigma(t))$ is future causal or zero for every $t\in[0,1]$.

**(b) Cone characterizations.**
$$J^+_C(p)=\exp_p(\mathcal C^+),\qquad I^+_C(p)=\exp_p(\mathcal T^+),\qquad J^+_C(p)\setminus\bigl(I^+_C(p)\cup\{p\}\bigr)=\exp_p(\mathcal N^+).$$

**(c) Null rigidity.** Let $\sigma:[0,1]\to C$ be future causal with
$\sigma(0)=p$, and let $\hat s\in(0,1]$ satisfy: $v(\sigma(\hat s))$ is
future null nonzero and $v(\sigma(t))\ne0$ for every $t\in(0,\hat s]$. Then
there are $v_0\in\mathcal N^+$ and a nondecreasing absolutely continuous
surjection $\varphi:[0,\hat s]\to[0,1]$ with
$\sigma(t)=\exp_p(\varphi(t)v_0)$ for $0\le t\le\hat s$.

**(d) Length maximality.** Let $\sigma:[0,1]\to C$ be future causal with
$\sigma(0)=p$. Then
$$L_g(\sigma)\le\sqrt{-D_p^2\bigl(\sigma(1)\bigr)}=\sqrt{-g_p\bigl(v(\sigma(1)),v(\sigma(1))\bigr)} .$$
If moreover $v(\sigma(1))$ is future timelike and $v(\sigma(t))\ne0$ for all
$t\in(0,1]$, then equality holds if and only if there are $v_0$ future
timelike and a nondecreasing absolutely continuous surjection
$\varphi:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ with $\sigma(t)=\exp_p(\varphi(t)v_0)$ for all $t$.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, and let $n$ be an observer at $p$
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]). For $w\in T_pM$ write
$h=h_n$ and $\gamma(w):=-g_p(n,w)$.

1. If $w$ is nonzero future causal, then $\gamma(w)>0$.
2. If $w$ is future unit timelike, then $\gamma(w)\ge1$, with
   $\gamma(w)=1$ if and only if $w=n$, and
   $g_p(h(w),h(w))=\gamma(w)^2-1$.
3. If $w$ is unit timelike, then $w$ is future-directed if and only if
   $g_p(n,w)<0$, and past-directed if and only if $g_p(n,w)>0$; in particular
   $g_p(n,w)\neq0$ for such $w$.

derivations.claim: (Existence of $B$ and the cone characterizations.) Choose a point-normal exponential-coordinate ball around $x$ with $\nabla u_x^0$ past timelike on it; the gradient is past timelike at $x$, and this is an open condition, so the ball of [[thm-gr-convex-normal-neighborhoods]] can be shrunk inside that region. The cone theorem now applies to every strictly convex normal set; it gives the cone characterizations in this chosen $B$ with base point $x$. The temporal-coordinate property is used separately below and is not a hypothesis of the cone theorem.

(No closed causal curves.) In the exponential chart $u$ of [L1], $\nabla u^0$ is past timelike throughout $B$. Thus $du^0(z)=g(\nabla u^0,z)>0$ for every nonzero future causal tangent $z$, by [L3]. Along a future causal curve the locally absolutely continuous composite $u^0\circ\gamma$ therefore has positive derivative almost everywhere. Integrating on $[0,1]$ gives $u^0(\gamma(1))>u^0(\gamma(0))$, so the endpoints cannot coincide. This proves (c) and also shows that a curve from $x$ has nonzero position vector at every positive parameter.

(Closedness and openness.) Under $\exp_x|_{W_x}$, the set $J_B(x)$ corresponds to the relatively closed cone $\{v\in W_x:g_x(v,v)\le0,\ g_x(v,N_x)\le0\}$, while $J_B(x)\setminus I_B(x)$ corresponds to $\{v\in W_x:g_x(v,v)=0,\ g_x(v,N_x)\le0\}$ including $v=0$. The future timelike cone is relatively open in $W_x$. The exponential map is a homeomorphism, so these facts prove (b) and the closed-set assertions of (e). Any limit of points in $I_B(x)$ or $\exp_x(\mathcal N^+)$ still belongs to the closed set $J_B(x)$; the limit need not stay in either of those smaller sets.

(Corner smoothing.) Let $\gamma$ have a future timelike derivative at $t_0\in[0,1]$ (with the appropriate one-sided derivative at an endpoint). Its final position vector is future causal by [L1], and nonzero by step 1.2. If that vector were null, [L1]'s null rigidity, with the nonvanishing supplied by step 1.2, would give $\gamma(t)=\exp_x(\varphi(t)v_0)$ on $[0,1]$ for a fixed future null $v_0$. The coefficient $\varphi$ is a linear coordinate of the smooth inverse exponential applied to $\gamma$, and hence is differentiable at $t_0$. Differentiating gives $\gamma'(t_0)=\varphi'(t_0)d(\exp_x)_{\varphi(t_0)v_0}(v_0)$, a null or zero vector by the radial-geodesic character in [L1], contradicting its timelike character. Thus the final position is future timelike, proving (d).
Claims (a)-(e) are the preceding steps, with (e) from the closedness step.

The singleton vertex is the reflexive part of J_B(x); step 1.2 excludes a nonconstant closed causal curve through it.
