boundaries.evidence: Individual compact shells may be empty and contribute no selected bumps; nonempty level points are covered by active shell neighborhoods in step 1.2.
The plateau gradient is allowed to vanish away from the middle level; the positive plateau integral A in step 1.3 is nonzero before division.
Statement boundary: At a level point one active timelike bump suffices: convexity of the past cone keeps a sum timelike when a timelike summand is present.

boundaries.reason: The metric remains Lorentzian; a zero gradient is explicitly permitted outside the timelike neighborhood of S_b.

boundaries.evidence: Statement boundary: The weak step takes exactly minus one below a and plus one above c, including equality at those outer levels; smooth gluing occurs where plateau formulas agree.
Countable Choice selects component base points and finite subcovers for countably many compact shells in step 1.2; its nonempty shells have cover witnesses.

boundaries.reason: The shell construction establishes a weak step, not an iff between past-causal gradient and global hyperbolicity.
An arbitrary weak step is not claimed to determine the shell cover or individual cone bumps in reverse.

risk_review.notes: Checked countable components and compact shells; repaired the uncountable preliminary bump selection using finite tuple covers per shell under AC_omega. Diameter<1 implies only finitely many selected tuples meet any component ball, hence smooth sums. Defined W canonically. Reversed bump supports are a locally finite closed union inside W; plateau gluing and quotient gradient give the weak step, including past/future flat plateaus. Statement unchanged; confidence 1.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]) for the actual volume-time and causal suppliers. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a globally hyperbolic
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (c)), let $t$
be the volume time function of [[thm-gr-volume-time-function]] with Cauchy
levels $S_c=t^{-1}(c)$, and let $a<b<c$ be real numbers. Then there is a
smooth function $\tau:M\to[-1,1]$ such that

**(a)** $\tau=-1$ on $\{t\le a\}$;

**(b)** $\tau=+1$ on $\{t\ge c\}$;

**(c)** $\nabla\tau$ is past causal or zero at every point of $M$: with the
gradient of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] one has
$g(\nabla\tau,\nabla\tau)\le0$ and $d\tau(N)=g(\nabla\tau,N)\ge0$;

**(d)** $\nabla\tau$ is past timelike at every point of $S_b$ and hence, by
continuity, on an open neighborhood of $S_b$: $g(\nabla\tau,\nabla\tau)<0$
and $g(\nabla\tau,N)>0$ there.

The function $\tau$ is a **weak step** around the level $b$: it moves from
the value $-1$ below the inner level $a$ to the value $+1$ above the outer
level $c$, with a timelike gradient near $S_b$ and a causal-or-zero gradient
everywhere.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). The cotangent space $T_p^*M$ is
the algebraic dual of $T_pM$ ([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]).

**Musical isomorphisms.** Define the **flat map**

$$\flat_p:T_pM\longrightarrow T_p^*M,\qquad \flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot),$$

so that $\flat_p(v)(w)=g_p(v,w)$; it is $\mathbb R$-linear by bilinearity of
$g_p$. Its kernel is $\{v:g_p(v,w)=0\text{ for all }w\}=\{0\}$ because $g_p$ is
nondegenerate, and $\dim_{\mathbb R}T_pM=\dim_{\mathbb R}T_p^*M=4$ since the
coordinate derivations of a chart form a basis of $T_pM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]); hence
$\flat_p$ is a linear isomorphism and has an inverse
$\sharp_p:T_p^*M\to T_pM$.

**Inverse metric.** The **inverse metric** at $p$ is the symmetric bilinear form

$$g_p^{-1}:T_p^*M\times T_p^*M\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta).$$

It is symmetric because $g_p$ is, and it is nondegenerate: if
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta)=0$ for all $\beta$, then $g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\cdot)=0$,
so $\sharp_p\alpha=0$ and hence $\alpha=0$.

**Components in a chart.** Let $(U,x)$ be a smooth chart and
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ the components of $g$; let
$dx^a|_q$ be the differential of the coordinate function $x^a$ at $q$
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]), so that
$dx^a|_q(\partial_b|_q)=\partial_b|_q(x^a)=\delta^a{}_b$. Define the components
of the inverse metric in this chart by

$$g^{ab}(q):=g_q^{-1}\bigl(dx^a|_q,\,dx^b|_q\bigr),\qquad q\in U,$$

so that $\sharp_q(dx^a|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)\,\partial_b|_q$; equivalently
$(g^{ab}(q))$ is the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab}(q))$ at every $q$, that is

$$g^{ac}(q)\,g_{cb}(q)=\delta^a{}_b,\qquad g_{ac}(q)g^{cb}(q)=\delta_a{}^b,$$

because $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=dx^a|_q(\partial_c|_q)=\delta^a{}_c$
and also $g_q(\sharp_qdx^a|_q,\partial_c|_q)=\sum_bg^{ab}(q)g_{bc}(q)$. In
particular $g^{ab}=g^{ba}$. The components $g^{ab}$ depend smoothly on $q$;
this is proved in [[lem-gr-inverse-metric-is-smooth]].

**Raising, lowering and metric trace.** Let $A$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on an open set $V\subseteq M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). At each $p\in V$ define the
endomorphism

$$A^\sharp_p:T_pM\to T_pM,\qquad A^\sharp_p(v):=\sharp_p\bigl(A_p(v,\cdot)\bigr),$$

characterized by $g_p(A^\sharp_p(v),w)=A_p(v,w)$ for all $w\in T_pM$; it is
self-adjoint for $g_p$ because $A_p$ is symmetric. Its **metric trace** is

$$\operatorname{tr}_g(A)(p):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(A^\sharp_p\bigr)$$

with the trace of an endomorphism as in [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. In a
chart the raised, mixed and doubly raised components are

$$A^{ab}:=g^{ac}g^{bd}A_{cd},\qquad A^a{}_b:=g^{ac}A_{cb},\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{tr}_g(A)=g^{ab}A_{ab},$$

the last identity obtained by evaluating in a $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, where $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ by
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] so that
$g^{ab}A_{ab}=\sum_a g^{aa}A_{aa}=-A(e_0,e_0)+A(e_1,e_1)+A(e_2,e_2)+A(e_3,e_3)$,
which is the trace of the endomorphism $v\mapsto\sharp_p(A_p(v,\cdot))$ in that
basis. All these operations are pointwise and depend only on $g$, $A$ and the
duality pairing, not on a chart.

**Conventions.** Raising and lowering apply to one index at a time and preserve
index order; $A_{ab}$, $A^a{}_b$ and $A^{ab}$ denote the same tensor $A$ with
indices positioned by $g$. The musical isomorphisms and the inverse metric are
defined for every smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of this library; no choice
principle is used in this definition, every ingredient being pointwise linear
algebra over $\mathbb R$ together with the pointwise nondegeneracy of $g_p$.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold $M$ admits a smooth nonnegative function $h:M\to[0,\infty)$ whose closed sublevel sets are compact. In particular $h$ is proper: the inverse image of each compact subset of $[0,\infty)$ is compact.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every smooth manifold admits a countable smooth atlas whose chart domains have compact closures.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{T}_d$ be
its metric topology ([[def-metric-topology]]), so that $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$ is a
topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and is metrizable
([[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. $(X,d)$ is a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]) **if and only
   if** $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$ is a compact topological space
   ([[def-compact-space]]).
2. For every $A \subseteq X$: $A$ is a compact subset of the metric space
   $(X,d)$ if and only if $A$ is a compact subset of the topological space
   $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$, the two readings of "compact subset" being the metric
   subspace $(A, d_A)$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]) and the topological
   subspace $(A, (\mathcal{T}_d)_A)$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Nothing here is a coincidence and nothing is transported.** The open-cover
condition of [[def-metric-compactness]] quantifies over families of subsets open
in $(X,d)$, and by [[def-metric-topology]] those are exactly the members of
$\mathcal{T}_d$; so the two conditions are not merely equivalent, they are the
same condition written twice. No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].

Let $X$ be a set and let $f_k:X\to\mathbb{R}$. Suppose there is a sequence of
nonnegative reals $(M_k)$ such that

$$|f_k(x)|\le M_k\qquad(k\in\mathbb{N},\ x\in X)$$

and the scalar series $\sum M_k$ converges. Then $\sum f_k(x)$ converges
absolutely for every $x\in X$, and the function series $\sum f_k$ converges
uniformly on $X$.

Let $a<b$ be reals and let $f_k:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuously
differentiable: each $f_k$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ and each derivative
$f_k'$ is continuous there ([[def-continuity-real]]). Suppose there is
$c\in[a,b]$ such that the real
sequence $(f_k(c))$ converges to $A$, and suppose $f_k'\to g$ uniformly on
$[a,b]$. Then there is a differentiable function $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ such
that

$$f_k\longrightarrow f\ \text{ uniformly},\qquad f'=g.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

derivations.claim: (Finite lists of weak steps for each compact slice.) For $j\ge1$ put $K_j:=L_j\cap\{a'\le t\le c'\}$, compact by [L3]. Consider all tuples $(b,\tau,U)$ with $b\in[a',c']$, $\tau$ a weak step supplied by [L1] with outer bounds $a,c$, and $U$ its open past-timelike-gradient locus containing $S_b$. Their open sets cover $K_j$, since at $x\in K_j$ a tuple exists with $b=t(x)$. Compactness supplies a finite tuple list covering $K_j$. For empty $K_j$, a single tuple at $b=(a'+c')/2$ is available, so every list may be taken nonempty. Countable Choice selects one nonempty finite list for each $j$. Write its entries $(b_{j,i},\tau_{j,i},U_{j,i})$, $1\le i\le m_j$. No weak-step family indexed by all real levels is selected.

(The averaged slice functions.) Define $v_j:= rac1{m_j}\sum_{i=1}^{m_j}	au_{j,i}$. Then $v_j$ is smooth, $v_j=-1$ on $\{t\le a\}$ and $v_j=+1$ on $\{t\ge c\}$ because every summand has these properties, $|v_j|\le1$, and $
abla v_j$ is past causal or zero everywhere as a finite average of past causal or zero vectors [L2]. On $K_j$ the gradient is past timelike: at $x\in K_j$ some $i$ satisfies $x\in U_{j,i}$, so $
abla	au_{j,i}(x)$ is past timelike and all other summands are past causal or zero, whence the finite sum $
abla v_j(x)$ is past timelike by [L2].

(Derivative bounds.) For each $j\ge1$ the set $\overline{B_1}\cup\cdots\cup\overline{B_j}$ is compact and the finitely many functions $\partial^\alpha v_j$, $|\alpha|\le j$, are continuous, so by [L5] each of them has a finite maximum there; let $A_j\ge1$ be an integer bounding all these maxima. Since $|v_j|\le1\le A_j$ as well, every coordinate derivative of $v_j$ of order at most $j$ is bounded by $A_j$ on the closures of the first $j$ boxes.

(The series.) Put $c_j:=2^{-j}A_j^{-1}$ and $C:=\sum_{j\ge1}c_j$, a positive real number with $C\le1$, and define $v:=\frac1C\sum_{j\ge1}c_jv_j$. On the box $B_i$, for every multiindex $\alpha$ and every $j\ge\max(i,|\alpha|)$ the bound of step 3.1 gives $\sup_{B_i}|\partial^\alpha(c_jv_j)|\le2^{-j}$, so by the Weierstrass M-test the series $\sum_jc_jv_j$ and each of its termwise coordinate derivative series $\sum_jc_j\partial^\alpha v_j$ converge uniformly on $B_i$; since the boxes cover $M$, this holds on every compact set after finitely many boxes. Applying the coordinate-line argument of [L4] inductively in the order of differentiation, $v$ is smooth on $M$ and every coordinate derivative of $v$ is the corresponding termwise derivative of the series.

(Properties of the series.) On $\{t\le a\}$ all summands equal $-1$, so $v=-1$; on $\{t\ge c\}$ they equal $+1$, so $v=+1$; and $|v|\le1$ because $C=\sum_jc_j$ and $|v_j|\le1$. Termwise differentiation gives $
abla v= rac1C\sum_{j\ge1}c_j
abla v_j$. Its partial sums lie in the closed past-causal cone by [L2], hence their limit is past causal or zero; this proves (b). Now fix $x$ in the inner strip and choose $j_0$ with $x\in L_{j_0}$. Then $x\in K_{j_0}$, so $c_{j_0}
abla v_{j_0}(x)$ is past timelike by step 2.1. The series of all remaining terms converges by step 4.1; its partial sums are past causal or zero by [L2], so its limit is past causal or zero by closedness of that cone. The sum of the fixed past-timelike vector and this limiting past-causal vector is past timelike by [L2]. Thus $
abla v(x)$ is past timelike, proving (c) without treating a limit of timelike vectors as timelike.

Step 3.1 takes A_j>=1, so c_j=2^(-j)/A_j is positive; the total C is positive before the normalized series in step 4.1.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]) for the actual volume-time and causal suppliers. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a globally hyperbolic
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (c)), let $t$
be the volume time function of [[thm-gr-volume-time-function]], and let
$a<a'<c'<c$ be real numbers. Then there is a smooth function
$v:M\to[-1,1]$ such that

**(a)** $v=-1$ on $\{t\le a\}$ and $v=+1$ on $\{t\ge c\}$;

**(b)** $\nabla v$ is past causal or zero at every point of $M$;

**(c)** $\nabla v$ is past timelike at every point of the inner strip
$\{a'\le t\le c'\}$.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]) for the actual volume-time and causal suppliers. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a globally hyperbolic
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (c)), let $t$
be the volume time function of [[thm-gr-volume-time-function]] with Cauchy
levels $S_c=t^{-1}(c)$, and let $a<b<c$ be real numbers. Then there is a
smooth function $\tau:M\to[-1,1]$ such that

**(a)** $\tau=-1$ on $\{t\le a\}$;

**(b)** $\tau=+1$ on $\{t\ge c\}$;

**(c)** $\nabla\tau$ is past causal or zero at every point of $M$: with the
gradient of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] one has
$g(\nabla\tau,\nabla\tau)\le0$ and $d\tau(N)=g(\nabla\tau,N)\ge0$;

**(d)** $\nabla\tau$ is past timelike at every point of $S_b$ and hence, by
continuity, on an open neighborhood of $S_b$: $g(\nabla\tau,\nabla\tau)<0$
and $g(\nabla\tau,N)>0$ there.

The function $\tau$ is a **weak step** around the level $b$: it moves from
the value $-1$ below the inner level $a$ to the value $+1$ above the outer
level $c$, with a timelike gradient near $S_b$ and a causal-or-zero gradient
everywhere.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]) for the curve calculus and auxiliary-length suppliers. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a globally hyperbolic
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (c)) and let
$\mu$ be the volume measure of [[lem-gr-finite-smooth-volume-density]] with
$\mu(M)=1$, $\mu(O)>0$ for every nonempty open $O$ and $\mu(E)=0$ for every
chart-Lebesgue-null Borel set. Let $L:=\ln$ denote the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]]) and define the **volume time function**
$$t:M\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad t(p):=L\bigl(\mu(I^-(p))\bigr)-L\bigl(\mu(I^+(p))\bigr) =\ln\frac{\mu(I^-(p))}{\mu(I^+(p))}.$$
Then:

**(a)** $t$ is well defined and continuous on $M$;

**(b)** $t$ is strictly increasing along causal relations: if $p\le q$
with $p\ne q$, then $t(p)<t(q)$; in particular $t$ is a time function in
the sense of [[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause
(d);

**(c)** for every inextendible future-directed causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ one has
$$\lim_{s\to\sup I}t(\gamma(s))=+\infty,\qquad \lim_{s\to\inf I}t(\gamma(s))=-\infty;$$

**(d)** every level set $t^{-1}(c)$, $c\in\mathbb R$, is a Cauchy set
([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (c)); in
particular it is acausal, and it is met in exactly one parameter value by
every inextendible causal curve.

No smoothness of $t$ is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]) for the absolutely continuous causal-curve
calculus and the supplied causal results used below.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]).
Call a map $x:I\to M$ a **geodesically connectible continuous causal curve**
when it is continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]) and for every strictly convex
normal ball $C$ as produced by [[thm-gr-convex-normal-neighborhoods]]
([[def-gr-normal-neighborhoods-and-position-vectors]] clause (b)) and all
$t_1<t_2$ in $I$ with $x([t_1,t_2])\subseteq C$, the endpoints $x(t_1)$ and
$x(t_2)$ are joined by a future causal geodesic whose image is contained in
$C$. Write $\le$ for the causal relation of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] (defined by locally absolutely
continuous future causal curves) and put
$$n:=\frac{N}{\sqrt{-g(N,N)}},\qquad h:=g+2\,n^\flat\otimes n^\flat .$$

**(a) Absolutely continuous implies connectible.** Every future causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ in the sense of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] is a
geodesically connectible continuous causal curve.

**(b) Connectible curves give causal relations.** Let $x:I\to M$ be a
geodesically connectible continuous causal curve and let $t_1<t_2$ in $I$.
If $x|_{[t_1,t_2]}$ is nonconstant, then for every open neighborhood $W$ of
$x([t_1,t_2])$ there is a piecewise smooth future causal curve
$\eta:[t_1,t_2]\to W$ with $\eta(t_1)=x(t_1)$ and $\eta(t_2)=x(t_2)$; in
particular $x(t_1)\le x(t_2)$. If the restriction is constant, its endpoints
coincide and reflexivity gives $x(t_1)\le x(t_2)$ without asserting a curve
in the nonconstant future causal class.

**(c) Equality of relations.** For $p,q\in M$ the following are equivalent:
$p\le q$; $p=q$ or there is a geodesically connectible continuous causal
curve with endpoints $p,q$.

**(d) One-sided extension.** Let $\gamma:[0,\infty)\to M$ be a
future-inextendible future causal curve in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (d). Then there is an
inextendible future causal curve $\gamma^*:I^*\to M$ with
$[0,\infty)\subseteq I^*\subseteq\mathbb R$ and $\gamma^*|_{[0,\infty)}=\gamma$;
that is, $\gamma$ is contained in a curve that is both future- and
past-inextendible. The dual statement holds for past-inextendible curves.

No choice principle beyond the stated assumptions is used. The extension in (d) is not asserted to be
unique.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal
classification of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and the
equivalence of "future-directed" with "pairing negatively with $N$" supplied by
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a continuous map,
where $I$ has its relative topology. A **chart representative** on a parameter
neighborhood $J\subseteq I$ is $x\circ\gamma|_J$, where $(U,x)$ is a smooth
chart and $\gamma(J)\subseteq U$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for each $t\in I$ there are
$\delta>0$ and a chart $(U,x)$ such that
$\gamma(I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta))\subseteq U$ and every coordinate of
$x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of
$I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta)$ in the sense of
[[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]. This includes one-sided neighborhoods
at included endpoints. Equivalently, for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the coordinates of $x\circ\gamma$ are
absolutely continuous on $[a,b]$. The equivalence and independence of the
chart and smooth atlas are proved in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]]
clause (a); continuity is part of both formulations.

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point: a
constant chart representative has derivative zero everywhere in its interior,
contradicting the full-measure nonzero-velocity requirement.

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ q\in J^+(p)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let $u$ be a temporal function
on it in the sense of [[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]]
clause (e), and write $\nabla u$ for its gradient. Then:

**(a)** $du(v)=g(\nabla u,v)>0$ for every nonzero future causal vector $v$.

**(b)** For every future causal curve $\gamma:I\to M$ in the class of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], the composite $u\circ\gamma$ is
locally absolutely continuous, its derivative satisfies
$(u\circ\gamma)'(t)>0$ at almost every $t\in I$, and consequently
$$u(\gamma(a))<u(\gamma(b))\qquad\text{whenever }a<b\text{ and }\gamma \text{ is not constant on }[a,b].$$

**(c)** $u$ is a time function on $(M,g,N)$ in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (d); every level
set $u^{-1}(c)$, $c\in\mathbb R$, is achronal; and $(M,g,N)$ is causal and
chronological: it admits no nonconstant future causal curve with equal
endpoints.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the
causal curves and the relations $\le$, $\ll$, $I^{\pm}$, $J^{\pm}$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]. All curves below are curves in
that sense.

**(a) Chronology and causality.** $(M,g,N)$ is **chronological** when there is
no $p\in M$ with $p\ll p$, equivalently when there is no nonconstant future
timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$. It is **causal**
when there is no nonconstant future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with
$\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$; a nonconstant future causal curve with equal endpoints
is called a **closed causal curve**, and a closed future timelike curve is
called a **closed timelike curve**.

**(b) Strong causality.** $(M,g,N)$ is **strongly causal** when for every
$p\in M$ and every open set $U\subseteq M$ with $p\in U$ there is an open set
$V$ with $p\in V\subseteq U$ such that for every future causal curve
$\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ and all $a\le s<t\le b$ with $\gamma(s)\in V$ and
$\gamma(t)\in V$ one has $\gamma([s,t])\subseteq V$. Thus no causal curve can
leave $V$ and later re-enter it; a set $V$ with this property for all causal
curves is called **causally convex for causal curves that meet it twice**.

**(c) Global hyperbolicity.** $(M,g,N)$ is **globally hyperbolic** when it is
strongly causal and for all $p,q\in M$ the **causal diamond**
$J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ is compact in the subspace topology
([[def-compact-space]]).

**(d) Time functions.** A **time function** on $(M,g,N)$ is a function
$u:M\to\mathbb R$ which is continuous from the manifold topology to the usual topology of
$\mathbb R$: for every $p\in M$ and every open neighborhood $W$ of $u(p)$
there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $p$ with $u(V)\subseteq W$
([[def-continuous-map-top]]). It also satisfies
$u(\gamma(a))<u(\gamma(b))$ for every future causal curve
$\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $a<b$ that is not constant on $[a,b]$.

**(e) Temporal functions.** A **temporal function** on $(M,g,N)$ is a smooth
function $u:M\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]])
whose gradient is past-directed timelike: writing $du$ for its differential
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]) and $\nabla u$ for the vector field
with $g(\nabla u,X)=du(X)$ for every smooth vector field $X$, constructed from
the inverse metric of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]], one
has
$$g(\nabla u,\nabla u)<0\qquad\text{and}\qquad du(N)=g(\nabla u,N)>0 .$$
The first inequality says that the gradient is nowhere zero and timelike; the
second fixes it as past-directed for the chosen time orientation. No level set
of a temporal function is asserted here to be a hypersurface or to be
spacelike, and no relation between temporal functions and compactness is
asserted; those claims are proved separately where they are used.

**(f) Scope and conventions.** These are mathematical conditions on the
Lorentzian model. Different sources define global hyperbolicity by equivalent
but differently phrased conditions; this page fixes the formulation of (c)
and proves the implications it uses. In particular no equivalence between
global hyperbolicity and the existence of a Cauchy hypersurface is asserted
by this definition, and the physical reading of strong causality or global
hyperbolicity as predictability of a classical model is adopted only in the
framework postulates.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. Components and closures refer to the topology obtained
by using any ordered basis to identify $V$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$;
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], step 5.1, proves that the
resulting open sets are independent of the basis. By that lemma the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth submersion and let $S\subseteq N$ be an embedded
submanifold of codimension $c$. Then $F^{-1}(S)$ is an embedded submanifold of
$M$ of codimension $c$. For each $p\in F^{-1}(S)$,

$$T_p\bigl(F^{-1}(S)\bigr)=(dF_p)^{-1}\bigl(T_{F(p)}S\bigr).$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the
causal curves of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], and let
$S\subseteq M$.

**(a) Spacelike hypersurfaces.** A subset $\Sigma\subseteq M$ is a **spacelike
embedded hypersurface** when it is an embedded three-dimensional submanifold
of $M$ ([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]) such that the
restriction of $g_p$ to $T_p\Sigma\times T_p\Sigma$ is positive definite for
every $p\in\Sigma$; equivalently, every nonzero vector tangent to $\Sigma$ is
spacelike ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). A spacelike
embedded hypersurface is automatically a nondegenerate hypersurface, so its
$g$-orthogonal complement in $T_pM$ is one-dimensional and nondegenerate, and
it carries a unique future-directed unit timelike normal; that normal is
constructed where it is used, not here.

**(b) Achronality and acausality.** $S$ is **achronal** when no two distinct
points $p,q\in S$ satisfy $p\ll q$ or $q\ll p$; $S$ is **acausal** when no two
distinct points $p,q\in S$ satisfy $p\le q$ or $q\le p$. Every acausal set is
achronal, since $p\ll q$ implies $p\le q$.

**(c) Cauchy sets.** $S$ is a **Cauchy set** when for every inextendible
causal curve $\gamma:I\to M$ the parameter set
$$\gamma^{-1}[S]:=\{t\in I:\gamma(t)\in S\}$$
has exactly one element. Because a strictly increasing continuous surjection
of intervals induces a bijection of parameter sets, this condition is
invariant under reparametrization
([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (e)); it is stated in terms of
parameters rather than of the point set $\gamma(I)\cap S$, so that a closed
causal curve counts two visits to the same point as two parameter values. A
**Cauchy hypersurface** is a Cauchy set that is also a spacelike embedded
hypersurface in the sense of clause (a).

**(d) Domains of dependence.** For any $S\subseteq M$ define
$$D^+(S):=\{p\in M:\text{every past-inextendible causal curve through }p \text{ meets }S\},$$
and dually $D^-(S):=\{p\in M:\text{every future-inextendible causal curve
through }p\text{ meets }S\}$, where "meets $S$" means that some parameter
value is mapped into $S$, and $D(S):=D^+(S)\cup D^-(S)$ is the **domain of
dependence** of $S$.

**(e) Cauchy horizon.** For a closed set $S\subseteq M$ the **future Cauchy
horizon** is
$$H^+(S):=D^+(S)\setminus I^-(D^+(S)),$$
the set of points of $D^+(S)$ that are not chronologically preceded by any
point of $D^+(S)$; dually $H^-(S):=D^-(S)\setminus I^+(D^-(S))$, and the
**Cauchy horizon** is $H(S):=H^+(S)\cup H^-(S)$.

**(f) Scope.** These are mathematical definitions. Neither existence of
Cauchy sets nor any relation between the objects defined here is asserted.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Two vectors $u,v\in V$ are
**$\eta$-orthogonal**, written $u\perp v$, when $\eta(u,v)=0$. For a subset
$S\subseteq V$ the **orthogonal complement** of $S$ is

$$S^{\perp}:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,s)=0\text{ for every }s\in S\},$$

and for a vector $u$ one writes $u^{\perp}:=\{u\}^{\perp}$.

**Elementary properties.** For every subset $S\subseteq V$:

- $S^{\perp}$ is a linear subspace of $V$: if $v,w\in S^{\perp}$ and
  $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, then for every $s\in S$ bilinearity gives
  $\eta(v+\lambda w,s)=\eta(v,s)+\lambda\eta(w,s)=0$, so $v+\lambda w\in S^{\perp}$.
  In particular the zero vector lies in $S^{\perp}$ and $S^{\perp}$ is never
  empty.
- $S\subseteq (S^{\perp})^{\perp}$: if $s\in S$, then $\eta(v,s)=0$ for every
  $v\in S^{\perp}$ by the definition of $S^{\perp}$, and symmetry of $\eta$
  gives $\eta(s,v)=0$ for every $v\in S^{\perp}$, that is,
  $s\in(S^{\perp})^{\perp}$.
- $S^{\perp}=(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}$: the inclusion
  $S\subseteq\operatorname{span}S$ gives
  $(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}\subseteq S^{\perp}$; conversely, if
  $v\in S^{\perp}$ and $u=\sum_i\lambda_i s_i$ is a finite linear combination
  with $s_i\in S$, then linearity in the second argument gives
  $\eta(v,u)=\sum_i\lambda_i\eta(v,s_i)=0$, so $v\in(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}$.

In particular, for every $u\in V$ one has $u\in u^{\perp}$ exactly when
$\eta(u,u)=0$, that is, exactly when $u$ is null or $u=0$
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

**A nonzero vector can be orthogonal to itself.** Take a basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal with
diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$; such a basis exists by clause 2 of the definition
of a Lorentz form. Then $v:=e_0+e_1$ is nonzero while
$\eta(v,v)=\eta(e_0,e_0)+2\eta(e_0,e_1)+\eta(e_1,e_1)=-1+0+1=0$, so
$v\in v^{\perp}$ with $v\neq 0$. This is exactly what fails for a
positive-definite inner product and is why orthogonal complements in a Lorentz
vector space need not be positive definite.

For every point $p\in M$ and every smooth vector field $X$ on $M$, there is a
unique maximal integral curve $\gamma_p:I_p\to M$ of $X$ with $\gamma_p(0)=p$.

A smooth vector field $X$ on $M$ is **complete** if, for every $p\in M$, the
maximal integral curve $\gamma_p$ of $X$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R$.

A smooth vector field $X$ on $M$ is complete if and only if its maximal flow
domain is all of $\mathbb R\times M$.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$.

A **local flow** of $X$ consists of an open set $\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R\times M$
containing $\{0\}\times M$ and a smooth map $\Phi:\mathcal D\to M$ such that:

1. $\Phi(0,p)=p$ for every $p\in M$;
2. for each $p$, the fibre $\mathcal D_p:=\{t:(t,p)\in\mathcal D\}$ is an
   interval;
3. for each $p$, the curve $t\mapsto \Phi(t,p)$ is an integral curve of $X$ on
   $\mathcal D_p$;
4. whenever both sides are defined,
   $\Phi(t,\Phi(s,p))=\Phi(t+s,p)$.

If $\mathcal D=\mathbb R\times M$, then $\Phi$ is the **global flow** of $X$.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $M$ be a smooth
manifold without boundary, let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]), let $p\in M$ and
let $\gamma:(\alpha,\beta)\to M$ be the unique maximal integral curve of $X$
with $\gamma(0)=p$ ([[thm-unique-maximal-integral-curve-through-each-point]],
[[def-integral-curve-of-a-vector-field]]). If $\beta<+\infty$ then for every
compact set $K\subseteq M$
([[def-compact-space]]) there is $s\in(\alpha,\beta)$ such that
$\gamma(t)\notin K$ for every $t\in(s,\beta)$. Dually, if $\alpha>-\infty$
then for every compact $K$ there is $s$ such that $\gamma(t)\notin K$ for
every $t\in(\alpha,s)$.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $X$ be a connected topological space ([[def-connected-space]]) and let
$f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]]), $\mathbb{R}$
carrying its usual topology ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
[[def-metric-topology]], [[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. $f[X]$ is an order-convex subset of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-interval]]).
2. **Intermediate values are attained.** If $p, q \in X$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   satisfies $f(p) \le c \le f(q)$, then there is $x \in X$ with $f(x) = c$.

Claim 2 is the intermediate value theorem with no hypothesis on $X$ beyond
connectedness: no order, no metric, no interval. The classical statement for a
continuous $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is the special case $X = [a,b]$, that
subspace being connected by [[cor-connected-subsets-of-the-line]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

derivations.claim: (Strip functions.) For every integer $j$ apply [L1] with the quadruple $a=j-2$, $a'=j-1$, $c'=j+1$, $c=j+2$, obtaining a smooth $\tau_j:M\to[-1,1]$ with $\tau_j=-1$ on $\{t\le j-2\}$, $\tau_j=+1$ on $\{t\ge j+2\}$ and $\nabla\tau_j$ past causal or zero everywhere and past timelike on the inner strip $\{j-1\le t\le j+1\}$. The countably many applications are made with $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

(The locally finite sum $T$.) Define $$T:=	au_0+\sum_{j\ge1} igl(	au_{-j}+	au_j igr).$$ The series is locally finite: choose $R>|t(x)|$ at a point $x$. On a neighborhood of $x$ one has $|t|<R$; if $j>R+2$, then $t<R<j-2$, so $	au_j=-1$ and (because $t\ge-R>-j+2$) $	au_{-j}=+1$ identically there, whence $	au_{-j}+	au_j=0$ on that neighborhood. By [[thm-a-locally-finite-sum-of-smooth-functions-is-smooth]] the sum $T$ is smooth, and $
abla T=
abla	au_0+\sum_{j\ge1}(
abla	au_{-j}+
abla	au_j)$ with only finitely many nonzero terms near any point. Every term is past causal or zero, so every partial sum is past causal or zero and so is the limit [L5]; at a point with $t(x)\in[k-1,k+1]$ for some integer $k$ the summand $	au_k$ has past timelike gradient and all others past causal or zero, so $
abla T(x)$ is past timelike by [L5]. Since $ igcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}[k-1,k+1]=\mathbb R$, the gradient $
abla T$ is past timelike everywhere; in particular $g(
abla T,
abla T)<0$ and $g(
abla T,N)>0$, so $T$ is a temporal function and (a) holds.

(The order bounds.) For every integer $k\ge0$ one has $T\ge2k+1$ on $\{t\ge k+2\}$ and $T\le-2k-1$ on $\{t\le-k-2\}$. Indeed on $\{t\ge k+2\}$ we have $\tau_0=+1$, $\tau_{-j}=+1$ for every $j\ge1$ (since $t\ge k+2\ge2\ge -j+2$), and $\tau_j=+1$ for $1\le j\le k$ (since $t\ge k+2\ge j+2$), while $\tau_j\ge-1$ always; hence $T\ge1+2k$. The past bound is the same computation with the signs reversed.

(The gradient field.) Define $X:=
abla T/g(
abla T,
abla T)$, smooth because the denominator is a nowhere-vanishing smooth function, and future-directed timelike because it is a negative multiple of the past-directed timelike $
abla T$ [L5]. Moreover $X(T)=dT(X)=g(
abla T,X)=g(
abla T,
abla T)/g(
abla T,
abla T)=1$.

(Divergence along causal curves.) Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be an inextendible future-directed causal curve. By [L2], $t(\gamma(s))\to+\infty$ as $s\to\sup I$; given an integer $k\ge0$, for all sufficiently large $s$ one has $t(\gamma(s))\ge k+2$, hence $T(\gamma(s))\ge2k+1$ by step 3.1. As $k$ is arbitrary, $T(\gamma(s))\to+\infty$; the past-directed case is dual. This is (c).

(Levels are Cauchy hypersurfaces.) By [L4] and step 2.1, $T$ is a time function: $T(\gamma(a))<T(\gamma(b))$ for every future causal curve not constant on $[a,b]$. Let $c\in\mathbb R$. Every inextendible causal curve meets $S_c:=T^{-1}(c)$ in at least one parameter value: for a future-directed curve, $s\mapsto T(\gamma(s))$ is continuous with limits $-\infty$ at the past end (dual of step 4.1) and $+\infty$ at the future end (step 4.1), so [L8] gives a parameter with value $c$; the past-directed case is dual. It meets $S_c$ at most once, because two distinct parameter values would give two causally related distinct points with equal $T$-value, contradicting strict monotonicity. Hence $S_c$ is a Cauchy set; in particular $T$ is surjective. Since $dT
e0$ everywhere (the gradient is timelike), $S_c$ is an embedded hypersurface by [L6], and its tangent space at $p$ is $\ker dT_p=(
abla T_p)^\perp$, which is positive definite because $
abla T_p$ is timelike [L6]. Hence $S_c$ is a spacelike embedded hypersurface and a Cauchy set, that is, a Cauchy hypersurface; this is (b).

(Completeness of $X$.) Let $\gamma:(\alpha,\beta)\to M$ be a maximal integral curve of $X$ with $\gamma(0)=z$. By the chain rule, $\frac{d}{ds}T(\gamma(s))=dT(X)(\gamma(s))=1$, so $T(\gamma(s))=T(z)+s$ throughout its domain. Suppose $\beta<+\infty$ and choose $s_0\in(\alpha,\beta)$. Define the smooth increasing bijection $\theta:[0,\infty)\to[s_0,\beta)$ by $\theta(u)=\beta-(\beta-s_0)e^{-u}$ and set $\widehat\gamma(u)=\gamma(\theta(u))$. This is a future causal curve. The escape lemma [L8] says the maximal flow line leaves every compact set as $s\to\beta$, so $\gamma(s)$ has no limit there; therefore $\widehat\gamma$ has no future endpoint limit and is future-inextendible. Apply the one-sided extension [[lem-gr-causal-curve-conventions]] clause (d) to obtain an inextendible future causal curve $\widehat\gamma^*$ which agrees with $\widehat\gamma$ on $[0,\infty)$. By step 4.1, $T(\widehat\gamma^*(u))\to+\infty$ as $u\to\infty$. But on this same tail $T(\widehat\gamma(u))=T(z)+\theta(u)\to T(z)+\beta<+\infty$, a contradiction. Hence $\beta=+\infty$; the time-reversed argument gives $\alpha=-\infty$. Therefore every maximal integral curve is defined on $\mathbb R$, so $X$ is complete by [L7]; its flow is global and smooth.

(The flow diffeomorphism.) Define $\Psi:\mathbb R\times S_0\to M$ by $\Psi(s,z):=\Phi(s,z)$. For $z\in S_0$ the curve $s\mapsto\Phi(s,z)$ is an integral curve of $X$ with $\Phi(0,z)=z$, so $T(\Phi(s,z))=T(z)+s=s$ by step 5.2; hence $\Psi$ takes values in $M$ with $T\circ\Psi(s,z)=s$. It is surjective: given $p\in M$, the point $z:=\Phi(-T(p),p)$ satisfies $T(z)=T(p)-T(p)=0$, so $z\in S_0$, and the composition law of the global flow gives $\Psi(T(p),z)=\Phi(T(p),\Phi(-T(p),p))=\Phi(0,p)=p$. It is injective: if $\Phi(s,z)=\Phi(s',z')$, applying $T$ gives $s=s'$, and then $z=\Phi(-s,\Phi(s,z))=\Phi(0,z')=z'$ by the inverse-time law. The inverse $p\mapsto(T(p),\Phi(-T(p),p))$ is smooth because $T$ and $\Phi$ are smooth. Hence $\Psi$ is a diffeomorphism, which is (e).

(The orthogonal product.) Put $ eta:=-1/g(
abla T,
abla T)$, a smooth positive function. Since $g(
abla T,
abla T)<0$ everywhere, $ eta>0$; and $X=
abla T/g(
abla T,
abla T)=- eta
abla T$, so $g(X,\cdot)=- eta\,g(
abla T,\cdot)=- eta\,dT$. Consequently $g(X,X)=- eta$ and $g(X,v)=0$ for every $v\in\ker dT$. Define the smooth symmetric tensor field $h_T:=g+ eta\,dT\otimes dT$. Then $h_T(X,\cdot)=g(X,\cdot)+ eta\,dT=- eta\,dT+ eta\,dT=0$, while for $v,w\in\ker dT$ one has $h_T(v,w)=g(v,w)$; since $\ker dT=(
abla T)^\perp$ is positive definite by [L6], $h_T$ restricts to a Riemannian metric on $\ker dT$. This proves the identity $g=- eta\,dT\otimes dT+h_T$ and the orthogonal decomposition of (f). Finally, differentiating $\Psi$ and using $d\Psi(\partial_s)=X$, $d\Psi(\partial_{z}v)=(d\Phi_s)_zv$ with $(d\Phi_s)_zv\in\ker dT$ by step 6.1, one obtains $\Psi^*g(\partial_s,\partial_s)=g(X,X)=- eta\circ\Psi$, $\Psi^*g(\partial_s,\partial_zv)=g(X,(d\Phi_s)_zv)=0$, and $\Psi^*g(\partial_zv,\partial_zw)=h_{(s,z)}(v,w)$; the last expression is positive definite because $(d\Phi_s)_z$ is a linear isomorphism onto $\ker dT_{\Phi(s,z)}$. This is (f), and it completes the proof.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and step 2.1: the integer-indexed weak-step family is nonempty; near any point only finitely many nonconstant paired terms survive cancellation.
Step 3.2 divides only by g(grad T,grad T)<0, proved in step 2.1. The metric coefficient beta is therefore positive and finite pointwise.
The level S_c has exactly one parameter meeting along each inextendible curve by step 5.1; every flow line meets S_0 once.

boundaries.reason: The temporal gradient is nowhere zero, so regular-level and orthogonal-complement arguments apply; a merely time function with critical points is insufficient.

boundaries.evidence: Step 5.2 excludes finite maximal flow endpoints using divergence of T; completeness is for the constructed normalized gradient field, not for an arbitrary temporal function.
Statement boundary: The integer family of strip functions uses the stated Countable/Dependent Choice premises; the normalized X is then uniquely determined by T.
The flow-product description in step 6.1 gives a unique zero-level point and time coordinate for each point, hence a diffeomorphism.
Conversely the flow product realizes every level as the corresponding time slice; step 7.1 computes the orthogonal metric pullback without mixed terms.
